## MONITUM IN EPISTOLAS TRES SEQUENTES.



## 1.

Tres epistolae sequentes inter pontificias litteras e veteri Vaticanae bibliothecae libro Romae primum editae, postea et a Baronio collatione earum facta cum altero codice ad annum 416 recusae sunt. Unde vero iis scribendis occasionem datam existimarit primus illarum editor, sic explicat: « Cum Joannes Hierosolymorum episcopus Origenis errores sequeretur, Hieronymus apud Bethleem degens, aliique permulti ab ejus communione abstinebant. Quam ob rem Joannis opera multis affecti sunt malis. » Veriorem autem illarum causam comperimus ex iis, quae Augustinus ad calcem libri de Gestis Pelagii narrat in hunc modum: « De his autem, quae post hoc judicium (Diospoli in Palaestina habitum) ibi a nescio quo cuneo perditorum, qui valde in [0598B] perversum perhibentur Pelagio suffragari, incredibili audacia perpetrata dicuntur, ut Dei servi et ancillae ad curam sancti Hieronymi pertinentes, sceleratissima caede afflicerentur, diaconus occideretur, aedificia monasteriorum incenderentur, vix ipsum ab hoc impetu atque incursu impiorum in Dei misericordia turris munitior tueretur, tacendum nobis potius video, et exspectandum quid illic fratres nostri episcopi de his tantis malis agendum existiment, a quibus eos dissimulare posse quis credat? » Ea enim quae in subjectis epistolis describuntur mala, Hieronymum minime ab Origenistis, sed a Pelagianis perpessum esse liquet.



## 2.

Ex eadem narratione discimus, horum haereticorum in monasterium Hieronymi curae commissum irruptionem post Diospolitanam synodum contigisse. Unde illud consequens est, ut nequaquam tunc evenerit, cum Hieronymus a Joannis communione abstinebat. Anno enim 415, mense Decembri labente, celebrata est Palaestina seu Diospolitana [0598C] synodus. Ab anno autem 397, Joannem Theophili Alexandrini opera cum Hieronymo reconciliatum esse eruditi probant. [n: (V. Tillem. tom. XII, p. 199.)] Indidem quoque manifestum est, epistolas sequentes minime ante annum 416 fuisse scriptas. Sed neque hoc anno illas multo posteriores esse Joannis mors anno 417 consignata persuadet. A Baronio ad finem [0599A] anni 416 referuntur. Verum eas in annum 417 differendas esse ipsi ex epistola 33 colligendum fuit. Aurelium enim, cui inscribitur haec epistola, et per quem Hieronymus litteras suas Innocentio tradi, ac vicissim Innocentius eas quibus Hieronymo rescribebat, ipsi reddi voluit; non alium esse censet ab episcopo Cathaginensi; nec ei hac in re ullus refragatur. At vero dum Aurelius iste cum collegis anno 417 ineunte ad Innocentium contra Pelagium atque Coelestium scriberet, Hieronymum ab horum haereticorum satellitibus quidquam passum esse ignorabat. Tunc tantum in Africa pervulgatum erat, Pelagium Hierosolymis constitutum multos ibi fallere, sed multo plures, ex quibus in epistola Milevitanae synodi Hieronymus unus appellatur, « adversus eum pro gratia Christi et catholicae fidei veritate confligere. » Certe postulabat hic locus, ut et id, quod novus gratiae Christi defensor ab impiis pertulerat, adjiceretur, si facinoris tam atrocis notitia in Africam pervenisset. Non ambigendum tamen, quin [0599B] acerrimus ille Hieronymi adversus Pelagium conflictus vera exstiterit causa, cur cum eo tam crudeliter actum sit. Quamvis igitur Eustochium et Paula violentiae monasterio suo illatae causam et auctorem reticuissent, Innocentio tamen de iis, quae Pelagius Hierosolymis actitabat, praemonito hoc subodorari difficile non fuit.

## 3.

Joannem Hierosolymitanum minacibus adeo litteris corripuit is papa, non solum, quia ejus erat tanta flagitia vel coercere vel vindicare; sed et quia eum illis favisse suspicio forte non deerat. Non latebant veteres inter illum et Hieronymum Origenis causa etsi jam pridem sopitae simultates. Fama quoque nuntiante audierat, quantum a Joanne Pelagius diligeretur. Quocirca ipsum Joannem Augustinus epist. 179, n. 1, sic alloquitur: « Pelagium vero fratrem nostrum, filium tuum, quem audio quod multum diligis; » et num. 5: « Si diligitis Pelagium, diligat vos etiam ipse, immo magis se ipsum, [0599C] et non vos fallat. »

## 4.

Demum observamus, epistolam Innocentii ad hunc Joannem Graecam phrasim sapere: adeoque hunc papam vel Graece scripsisse, vel certe ut quod Graece scripserat in latinum converteretur, curasse, ac solam hujus Graeci textus interpretationem Latinam litterae valde tenacem ad nos pervenisse. Sane unus et alter locus, qui prima specie obscuri vel etiam manci apparent, ad Graecam phrasim exacti, statim perspicui et integri evadunt.

Quoniam ergo certa definitione monstratum est, qui debeant admitti, quive reprobari: ex his omnibus, quos videt dignatio tua non posse reprobari, eligere debebis quos clericos facias. ## EPISTOLA XLII. SEU LITTERARUM PELAGII AD PAPAM INNOCENTIUM, POST MORTEM EJUS, SED CUM EUM DEFUNCTUM NESCIRET, SCRIPTARUM FRAGMENTA.



## 1.

*In his, teste Augustino [n: (Lib. de Gratia Christi, c. 30)]*, *Pelagius dicit,* esse de quibus eum homines infamare conantur: unum, quod neget parvulis baptismi sacramentum, et absque redemptione [0608B] Christi aliquibus coelorum regna promittat: aliud, quod ita dicat posse hominem vitare peccatum, ut Dei excludat auxilium, et in tantum libero confidat arbitrio, ut gratiae repudiet adjutorium.

## 2.

*Prosequitur Augustinus [n: (Ibid., c. 31)]*: *His cum invidiosas de inimicis suis admiscuisset querelas, ad rem ita venit:* Ecce apud beatitudinem tuam epistola ista me purget, in qua pure atque simpliciter ad peccandum et ad non peccandum integrum liberum arbitrium habere nos dicimus, quod in omnibus bonis operibus divino adjuvatur semper auxilio.

## 3.

*Deinde, inquit Augustinus [n: (Ibid.,)]*, *cum de hominis conditione, et ad peccandum atque non peccandum naturali ejus possibilitate quaedam interposuisset, adjunxit:* [0609A] Quam liberi arbitrii potestatem dicimus in omnibus esse generaliter, in Christianis, in Judaeis atque Gentilibus. In omnibus est liberum arbitrium aequaliter per naturam: sed in solis Christianis juvatur a gratia. In illis nudum et inerme est conditionis bonum: in his vero qui ad Christum pertinent, Christi munitur auxilio. Illi ideo judicandi atque damnandi sunt, quia cum habeant liberum arbitrium, per quod ad fidem venire possent, et Dei gratiam [cn: a | In haec verba Augustinus: << Nempe, inquit, manifestum est, eum dicere gratiam secundum merita dari, quamlibet eam vel qualemlibet significet; quam tamen aperte non exprimit. >>] promereri, male utuntur libertate concessa. Hi vero remunerandi sunt, qui bene libero utentes arbitrio, merentur Domini gratiam, et ejus mandata custodiunt.



## 4.

Item adversarios suos ad librorum, quos pridem conscripserat, lectionem provocabat his verbis [0609B] [n: (Ibid., c. 35)]: « Legant illam epistolam [cn: b | His rursum subdit Augustinus: << Hanc ego legi; et inveni eum pene per totam non immorari nisi in facultate et possibilitate naturae, et pene ibi tantum Dei gratiam constituere. Christianam vero gratiam tanta brevitate perstringit, ut nihil aliud videatur, quam eam tacere timuisse. >>], quam ad sanctum virum Paulinum episcopum ante duodecim fere annos scripsimus, quae trecentis forte versibus nihil aliud quam Dei gratiam et auxilium confitetur, nosque nihil omnino boni facere posse sine Deo. Legant etiam epistolam [cn: c | Hanc reperire se non potuisse Augustinus testatur. << Sed si, inquit, non est dissimilis caeteris, non habet etiam ipsa quod quaerimus. >>] ad sanctum Constantium episcopum [n: (Ibid., c. 36)], ubi breviter quidem, sed plane libero hominis arbitrio Dei gratiam auxiliumque conjunxi. Legant etiam quam [cn: d | De hac ita idem Doctor loquitur: << Istam sane legi, mihique pene persuaserat, hanc illum gratiam, de qua quaestio est, confiteri. Sed cum in manus meas et alia venissent, quae posterius latiusque conscripsit, vidi quemadmodum potuerit etiam illic gratiam nominare, sub ambigua generalitate quid sentiret abscondens, gratiae tamen vocabulo frangens invidiam offensionemque declinans. >> In hoc autem Pelagii opere virus latens retexit Augustinus epist. olim 143, nunc 188, ad Julianam, ad cujus epistolae calcem hanc Pelagii ad Innocentium, immo et hunc ipsum locum non obscure notat ubi ait: << In quadam vero epistola sua idem Pelagius, ubi et nomen suum apertissime ponit, nec nomen sacrae virginis tacet, dicit ad eam se scripsisse, et ejusdem sui operis testimonio probare nititur, se gratiam Dei, quam vel tacere vel negare asseritur, apertissime confiteri. >>] ad sacram Christi virginem Demetriadem in Oriente conscripsimus [n: (Ibid., c. 37)]: et invenient nos ita hominis laudare naturam, ut Dei semper gratiae addamus auxilium. Legant etiam recens meum [cn: e | De opusculo hoc ea est Augustini censura. << Quatuor sunt libri operis hujus, et hos legi... Sed in his etiam quatuor libris quaecumque pro gratia videtur dicere, qua juvamur ut declinemus a malo bonumque faciamus, ita dicit, ut nullo modo a verborum ambiguitate discedat quam discipulis sic possit exponere, ut nullum auxilium gratiae credant, qua naturae possibilitas adjuvetur, nisi in lege atque doctrina. >> Et paucis intermissis: << Sed hoc adjutorium legis atque doctrinae etiam propheticis fuisse temporibus, adjutorium autem gratiae, quae proprie gratia nuncupatur, in Christi esse arbitratur exemplo; quod nihilominus ad doctrinam pertinere perspicitis, quae nobis evangelica praedicatur. >>] opusculum [n: (Ibid., c. 41)], quod pro libero nuper arbitrio edere compulsi sumus: et agnoscent quam inique nos negatione [0609C] gratiae infamare gestierint, qui per totum pene ipsius textum operis perfecte atque integre et liberum arbitrium confitemur et gratiam. » [0610A]

## 5.

Sed et ab his litteris ad fidei suae librum, quem iis subnexuerat, vult transire lectorem [n: (Ibid., c. 32)]. Is porro fidei liber totus insertus Sermoni alias Augustini de Tempore 191, nunc append. 236, n. 2 et seqq. ac praeterea seorsim editus est in appendice to. X novae editionis ejusdem sancti, pag. 96, sicut et apud Hieronymum, cui olim ascriptus fuerat.

## 6.

Praeterea in litteris illis, « quas, » inquit Augustinus [n: (lib. de Peccato origin., n. 19, 20 et 21)] , « Romam misit ad beatae memoriae papam Innocentium, et quoniam in corpore eum non invenerunt, sancto papae Zosimo datae sunt, et ad me directae, hoc est in eadem epistola, querebatur » se ab hominibus [cn: f | Ad haec Augustinus loco citato: << Non sic illis haec objiciuntur, ut posuit. Nam neque parvulis negant baptismi sacramentum, nec absque redemptione Christi aliquibus coelorum regna promittunt... Objicitur autem illis, quod non baptizatos parvulos nolunt damnationi primi hominis obnoxios confiteri. >>] infamari, quod neget parvulis baptismi sacramentum, et absque redemptione Christi aliquibus [0610B] coelorum regna promittat. » Et cum dixisset, « numquam se vel impium aliquem haereticum audisse, qui hoc de parvulis diceret, » subjiciebat: « Quis enim ita evangelicae lectionis ignarus est, qui hoc non modo affirmare conetur, sed qui vel leviter dicere aut etiam sentire possit? Deinde quis tam impius, qui parvulos exsortes regni coelorum esse velit, dum eos baptizari et in Christo renasci [cn: g | Ista Pelagii verba in medium prolaturus Augustinus, praemittit: << Videte latebras ambiguitatis falsitati praeparare refugia, offundendo caliginem veritati; ita ut etiam nos, cum primum ea legimus, recta vel correcta propemodum gauderemus. Sed latiores, inquit, disputationes ejus in libris, ubi se quantumlibet operiat, plerumque aperire compellitur, fecerunt nobis et ista suspecta, ut attentius intuentes inveniremus ambigua. >>] vetat, et in perpetuam certamque vitam renasci [cn: h | Circa horum verborum intelligentiam quantum laborarit Augustinus ubi explicuit, adjicit: << Tam sunt ambigua, ut possint eorum dogmati praebere latibula, unde ad insidiandum prosiliat haereticus sensus. >>] vetet eum, qui natus sit ad incertam. »

## 7.

Simul cum Pelagii praedictis litteris ac libello fidei ad Innocentium missa est, simulque Innocentii successori Zosimo reddita epistola Praylii Hierosolymitani episcopi, de qua hoc unum a Zosimo discimus, quod in ea Praylius Joannis successor causae [0610C] Pelagii enixius adstipulator intervenit [n: (Epist. 3, n. 2)].

## 8.

Qui autem praedicta legerit litterarum Pelagii [0611A] fragmenta, necnon Augustini, qui omnes vafri hujus haeretici artes ac subterfugia probe noverat, subnexas observationes expenderit, audieritque simul eumdem Hierosolymitani antistitis commendatione probatum atque laudatum esse; is sane Zosimum, simpliciter verba illius ut sonabant accipientem, decipi ab eo potuisse minus mirabitur.

## MONITUM IN FRAGMENTUM SEQUENS.[n: (Spicileg. Maii, tom. III.)]

Superioribus epistolis Innocentii I vulgatis saepe subnectimus latiorem partem ex ejus inedita epistola ad Severianum Gabalorum episcopum. Equidem in codice Arabico non *Gabala* sed *Haiala* scribitur, quae lectio vim quamdam accipit ex eo quod *Aila* episcopalis est urbs Palaestinae apud Lequinium Or. ch. t. III, p. 758; sed tamen in paucissimis quos [0611B] Lequinius novit ejus urbis episcopis, Severianus non censetur. Statim igitur de Severiano Gabalorum, urbis item Syrae, episcopo cogitavi, qui contemporaneus fuit Innocentio; quodque magis interest in notitia epistolarum Innocentii deperditarum apud Constantium p. 921 cognoscimus, inter Severianum et Innocentium epistolas missitatas fuisse. Praeterea paulo infra in codice Arabico fragmentum item Severiani legitur, quo loco non *Haiala,* sed *Gabala* sedes ejus episcopalis dicitur. Mendum igitur Arabici codicis ex litterulae similitudine coortum est. Hoc ergo epistolare Innocentii fragmentum ab Arabe homine nobis conservatum gratanter accipiamus.

## EPISTOLA XLIII. SEU FRAGMENTUM EPISTOLAE QUAM AD SEVERIANUM EPISCOPUM SCRIPSIT INNOCENTIUS UNUS EX PRIMIS ROMAE EPISCOPIS.

[0611C]Cum divinum e coelis Verbum advenit, et in Virginis sanctae Mariae visceribus, de qua carnem sumpsit, habitavit, nequaquam corpus suum de coelo [0612A] secum detulit, neque suam in terris divinitatem adeptus est; sed ipse Deus erat, ipse corpus suum in Virginis utero efformavit; neque ullum in suo corpore conficiendo socium habuit, sed unus ipse confecit. Confitemur autem in omnibus quae ab humanitate fiebant, comitem fuisse divinitatem, quae nullo umquam vel minimo temporis articulo ab humanitate sejuncta fuit. Confitemur etiam, eo ipso tempore quo noster e coelis Servator advenit, atque in Virginis Mariae uterum descendit, divinitatem cum humanitate conjunxisse, quae numquam ulla in re vel actione divisae fuerunt, quandoquidem indivisibiles erant. Ac veluti ejus divinitas fine caret, ita et ejusdem humanitas post resurrectionem in aeternum manet. Lac de femina suxit, nihilominus divinitas [0612B] atque humanitas unum ( *Christum* ) constituebant. Nec quisquam putet, quo tempore divinum in terris Verbum ad suscipiendum abs Joanne baptismum accessit, tunc initium divinitatis ejus fuisse, cum videlicet vocem Patris e coelo exeuntem Joannes audivit. Haud sane ita res se habet; verum ipso temporis articulo, quo in uterum Virginis descendit, unum cum corpore et divinitate individuum effectum est; fuitque divinitas corporis consors, atque immutabili quadam ratione et inseparabili facta est unica unitas. Divinitas ab humanitate non est sejuncta. Christo in cruce existente, divinitas ab ejus humanitate non secessit. In coelum ascendit cum corpore quod de Virgine Maria sumpsit, atque ad optimi Patris sui dexteram sedit. Haec fides nostra [0612C] est. Qui autem non ita credunt, eos catholica Ecclesia expellit, immo auctor ejusdem Deus excommunicat. Laus Deo in aeternum! Amen.

## [nt: This is one of those letters which Holstenius published in the first part of the *Roman Collection*, inserted in the acts of the Roman synod under Boniface II. Since Innocent calls this letter the *first-fruits* of his episcopate, which he entered upon *at once* on the death of Anastasius, we may not without reason conclude that it was written about the month of May of the year 402.] EPISTLE I, OF POPE INNOCENT I TO ANYSIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA. *Innocent confirms to Anysius that authority over the Churches of Illyricum which Anastasius and his predecessors had granted him.*

[0463D]

*To his most beloved brother ANYSIUS, INNOCENT.*

Since our God Christ has deigned to call to himself the man of holy memory, Bishop Anastasius, albeit swiftly, [0464D] reckoning his merits to be so great and of such a kind that they already exceeded the fellowship of human conversation, and that age, by reason of the purity of his life and the abundance of his teaching, with which he ruled the people of God with the whole rigour of ecclesiastical authority: lest his Church should remain even a little while without the helm of a ruler, at once, according to his mercy, with the consent of the holy priests and of all the clergy and people, with the peace which God, returning to heaven, [0465A] deigned to bestow on his Church, it was fitting to recognize me ordained in his place, dearest brother [n: ( f. te cognoscere)]; and to announce my first-fruits swiftly to none but a man [nt: The same Anysius is honoured by Palladius, in the *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*, ch. 3, with the encomium of *an excellent old man*, τοῦ χαλογήρου. There it is also recorded that he entrusted his own letter as well to Eulysius, bishop of Apamea in Bithynia, who was carrying to Rome the letters of fifteen bishops in support of Chrysostom.] most excellent and ever faithfully labouring in God [n: (V. epist. 2 Nicolai I)]. To whom also my predecessors in the episcopate before me, men so great and of such a kind, that is, Damasus of holy memory, Siricius, and the man mentioned above, so deferred, that they committed to thy holiness, which is full of justice, the cognizance of all things that were done in those parts; it becomes thee to recognize that my littleness also holds this judgment and has the same will. For it was not right either that I should attempt to go against the judgment of men so great and so good, into whose place I am known to have succeeded, or that anything should seem to be taken away from thy merit, on which illustrious men [0465B] are seen to have conferred so great a favour of this authority. I therefore openly declare that I acknowledge this very thing to be reserved to my littleness also: that with equal judgment and in like form I grant, both to the good alike and to thy charity, that which thou deservest.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER.



## 1.

*The things in it copied from Siricius do not make its authenticity doubtful.* --Many things in this letter are copied from Letter 4 of Siricius. But, as Tillemont observed, this ought not to seem at all surprising, since Innocent, asked by Victricius to hand on to him the rules customarily kept in the Roman Church, could not have done this more happily than by copying out the decrees of his predecessors. Hence, therefore, no fit reason is found why either the aforesaid letter should be taken away from Siricius, or this one from Innocent. Nor are the grounds lighter which assign this one [0465C] to Innocent than were those which assign that one to Siricius. It is cited under his name by the Second Council of Tours, c. 20, by Cresconius in the *Breviarium canonum* passim, and by Pope Zacharias in Sirmond, tome I of the *Concilia Galliae*, Epistle 9, cc. 14 and 20. Moreover, of the old collections, of which we have examined a great many, in none is it lacking, in none is it not presented inscribed to Innocent. It is ascribed to him by the Corbie exemplar copied in the times of Pope Vigilius, by the Colbert one written in Lombardic capital letters, by the old Codex of canons published by Quesnel, by the exemplars of the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections, and also by the Spanish collection, the Isidorian, and many others.

## 2.

*That it is not to be put back to the year 405.* --In all these collections [nt: (if you except the Dionysian, in which the consular date is omitted)] the ending of the letter is entirely the same, and with the greatest agreement it is dated *Honorio aug.* VI *et Aristeneto conss.* Hence no room is left for the conjecture of a learned man, by which he suspects that this consular date was added to this letter of Innocent [0465D] by another hand, or at any rate that *post consulatum Honorii*, etc., should be read. For though we grant him that the words *post consulatum*, which copyists are accustomed to express by the first letters *P. C.*, could easily have fallen out; in that case surely *Honorii et Aristeneti*, not *Honorio et Aristeneto*, would have been retained in at least some old codex, nor ought the word *conss.* to have been added in any. Nor shall we be any more compelled to yield to that conjecture if we weigh what cause there may be why he thinks this letter written in the year 405 rather than 404. He is moved, namely, solely by the words of no. 5, in which Innocent mentions what he had endured on account of the curials, with the emperor present, and with Victricius placed beside him. From which he also thinks it follows that this letter was written not only after the emperor had come into the City, [0466A] but also after Victricius had returned from Rome to Rouen. And yet, he says, the Emperor Honorius came to Rome only in the year 403, in the month of December, and had not come there before, as is gathered from Claudian's poem: and Victricius, in so small an interval as runs from the emperor's arrival in the City to the 15th day of February of the year 404, could not return from Rome to Rouen, and send a letter thence to Innocent, so that it was delivered to him before that day. From which he concludes that this letter was dated not in the consulship of Honorius Augustus, but after the consulship of Honorius Augustus, that is, in the year 405, not 404. But if, on account of a fact of which no certain knowledge is had, it be lawful to deny credit to titles so many, so diverse and so ancient, what will be certain in history? Let it be, then, that Honorius came to Rome at the close of the year 403, and that Victricius was in the City at that time: what compels us to agree at the same time that the same bishop had returned to Rouen before he received this letter of Innocent? Innocent mentions no one sent to him in Victricius's name, no [0466B] letter of his delivered to him. But, says the learned man, the word *misi*, which Innocent uses in the opening, implies one who is absent. But if it implies one absent, it certainly does not signify one returned to Rouen, not one gone out of Rome. For what prevents Victricius, about to depart [sic: *asbcessurus*] from Rome, from having asked of him a book of the ecclesiastical rules while he was bidding Innocent farewell, and him, not having the book at hand at that time, from having taken care that it should be put together as soon as possible and delivered to Victricius before his departure from the City. Nor indeed is it necessary that those to whom we are said to send something should be far from us. Friends daily send one another little gifts, books, letters, etc., even when contained within the walls of the same city. Let Damasus and Jerome be an example of this, above, p. 579 and following.

## 3.

*It is called the book of rules. The division of the chapters.* --Further, the book of rules mentioned does not seem to be reckoned anything other than this very letter, inasmuch as in it Innocent, after a brief preface, sets out several chapters of discipline [0466C] by which Churches are to be ruled. These chapters, moreover, are presented summarily in most manuscripts, though not in all, with titles set before them. But neither in those is this division or summary of the chapters one and the same; rather it varies according to the bent and judgment of those who collected the pontifical letters. More ample than the rest, however, is the one which the exemplars of the Codex published by Quesnel present. Wherefore we should have held it enough to represent that one alone here, were it not worth the labour to add to it the other, from the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, with which the Spanish collection too, from which the Isidorian was copied, agrees in nearly everything. For since Cresconius and other collectors of canons are accustomed to cite the decrees of the Roman pontiffs according to the division into titles arranged by Dionysius, it is necessary, in order that their citations may be found, to know beforehand what that division is. Now Dionysius Exiguus comprised in twenty-nine titles all the decrees which he collected from Innocent, among which the first place is held by this pope's letter to Decentius, divided into eight [0466D] titles. Then this one to Victricius follows it, which he divides into twelve titles. Wherefore the first decree of this letter is called title 9 in Dionysius, and the last title 20, as is to be seen below.



## 4.

*The laws which forbade curials to move out of the curia.* --In those decrees, moreover, that which is said in cap. 11 about the curials must be explained here somewhat more fully than is permitted in the annotations, because mention of the same matter will occur again and again in other letters of other pontiffs as well. Those were called curials, or decurions, who discharged the municipal magistracies and offices. Of them the Emperor Majorian, at the beginning of Novel 1, speaks thus: « No one is unaware that the curials are the sinews [0467A] of the commonwealth and the vitals of the cities: whose body antiquity rightly called the lesser Senate. » But, as the same emperor observes, the judges or governors of the provinces reduced many by their unjust exactions to such a point that they deserted their native place. To the curials belonged the charge of taxes, of buildings, of public shows or games, etc. For this reason the laws of the emperors were severe, by which no one was permitted to be freed from the curia unless he had discharged all the offices of his curia. The Emperor Constantine ordained [n: (Cod. Th. lib. XII, tit. 1, leg. 11)]: « Let no judge attempt to grant to any curial exemption from civil duties, or free anyone from the curia at his own discretion: » Of those too who, leaving their curias, take refuge in the garrisons of the army, he orders [n: (Leg. 1)] « all who are not yet found liable to the primipilate to be released from the army and to return to the curia. » Likewise he laid down [n: (Leg. 12)], as the interpreter Anianus puts it, « that whatever curial wishes to pass from the city in which he was born to another, may in no way [0467B] . . . nor by any plea of necessity escape the condition owed to the curia, or the services of his own city, on the ground that he wished to change his city. » By another law too [n: (Leg. 20)] he commands « that no curial, unless all the offices of the curia have been performed in order (Anianus adds, *which are owed to the native place*), ought to undertake the office of curator or defensor. » Nor was the indulgence of the emperors any greater towards those who migrated from the curia to the clergy. Ambrose, Epistle 41, to the Emperor Theodosius, n. 29, thought he must remonstrate with him on this matter in this manner: « How shall I excuse myself before the bishops, who now lament grievously because certain men who have discharged the rank of presbyter, or ministers of the Church, through thirty and innumerable years, are dragged back from the sacred office and assigned to the curia? » And that remonstrance was all the more just because Constantine had earlier [n: (Leg. 13)] wished the curias to be admonished that henceforth « they should drag back to the curia only those whom they found, within twenty years' service in the offices, either to have fled their origin, [0467C] or to have spurned nomination and thrust themselves into the service. » Indeed Julian had afterwards decreed [n: (Leg. 56)]: Those who, born of curial origin, have loved the military office, when the service of ten years has been completed, shall by the authority of our commands be exempt from the curia.

## 5.

*On what condition curials were permitted to give their names to the clergy.* --Curials were not so removed from the clergy that every approach to it was closed to them. Valentinian and Valens permit them to give their names to the clergy on a certain condition, which they explain thus in a law given in the year 364, on the 10th day of September [n: (Leg. 59)]: « He who chooses the part of the Church, let him either, by conferring his own goods on a kinsman, make him a curial in his stead, or cede his means to the curia which he has left, he who has done neither being of necessity recalled: » that is, so that he who did not cede his goods either to a kinsman or to his curia is by all means to be recalled to the curia. On the same matter there is also this constitution of Theodosius, dated the year 384, on the 7th day of November [n: (Leg. 104)]: « Curials who prefer to serve the churches rather than the curias, if they wish [0467D] to be what they feign, let them despise those things which they withdraw. For we free them on no other terms than that their patrimonies be despised. » Ambrose had this in view when he wrote in Epistle 18, to Valentinian, n. 13: « If a priest seek the privilege of declining the curial burden, he must give up the possession of his paternal and ancestral property and of all his means. » Constantius had been somewhat more indulgent: for in the year 361, on the 29th day of August, he first decreed in favour of the bishops [n: (Leg. 49)]: « Let no one compel a bishop only to make over his means to the curia, as had formerly been laid down. » Then he wills that those should enjoy the same privilege « who have attained the ranks of presbyters, and of deacons also, or subdeacons and the rest, with the curia assisting, and giving its consent under the eye of the judge . . . above all if they are asked for by the voices of the whole people. » Otherwise he orders [0468A] that two portions of their substance be handed over, either to their kinsmen substituted for the curial duties, or to the curia; but reserves the third to themselves. And of those who had failed of the conditions set out above, what is added at the end of the same constitution seems to have been said: « If the superintendents of the granaries, and those who are about to undertake a magistracy, the superintendents of the peace also, or the receivers of the various kinds of goods, have thought they should aspire to the Church (that is, to the ministry of the Church), after they have entered upon the offices of the charge or honour laid on them; it will be fitting for the prelates of the heavenly law first to resist them, and, they themselves being the first to strive for it, for these to be recalled to the same duties: or if they neglect this, they are to be dragged back by the curials, with the judgment of the office supporting. » Indeed Arcadius, derogating from his father's law, issued a constitution dated the year 398, on the 27th day of July, and reported in the *Codex Justinianus*, book I, tit. 3, law 12, by which he orders that a curial, if he has been ordained a cleric, be restored at once upon prior summons: « For we do not suffer, he says, that law to profit clerics any longer which, upon cession of patrimony having followed, did not forbid decurions to be clerics. » That this, however, was said of the minor [0468B] clerics alone is proved by what the same emperor laid down at the close of the year 399 [n: (Leg. 163)]: « If any, from our father's second consulship, leaving the curia, have made themselves over to the fellowship of the clergy, if they have already been found worthy to be bishops, or presbyters, or deacons, let them indeed persevere in the sacred and more secret mysteries; but let them be compelled either to offer substitutes to the curia, or, according to the law long since passed, to hand over their means to the curia. All the rest, readers, subdeacons, or clerics to whom the privileges of clerics are not owed, are to be presented forthwith to the duties owed to their native place. » With laws so many and so diverse, therefore, the judges did not lack an occasion by which to reclaim importunately curials admitted into the clergy, and thereby to make trouble for the prelates of the churches.

## EPISTLE II. From an old Colbert exemplar, no. 932.






## I.

*That no one of the bishops dare to ordain without the knowledge of the metropolitan [0468C] bishop.* --II. *That he who has chosen to have the belt of military service after the remission of sins be not admitted to the clergy.* --III. *That all contentions or causes arising among clerics of any order be ended before the provincials, that is, their own bishops. That the greater causes be referred to the apostolic see after the episcopal judgment.* -- IV. *That a cleric take a virgin to wife.* --V. *That a layman who has taken a widow to wife, whether before baptism or after baptism, be not admitted to the clergy.* --VI. *That he who has married a second wife ought not to be ordained a cleric, even if he obtained (such) a marriage before baptism.* --VII. *That no one presume to ordain a cleric from another's church.* --VIII. *That those baptized who come from the Novatians or the Montenses be received by [0468D] the imposition of hands only.* --IX. *That priests and levites do not come together with their wives.* --X. *That a monk, if he wishes to strive for the order of the clergy, ought not to turn aside from the prior purpose which he bore as a monk.* --XI. *That he who, being corrupted, wishes to come to the clergy, promise not to take a wife, according to the rule of the ancients.* --XII. *That curials, or those occupied with any public functions whatever, be not made clerics.* --XIII. *That handmaids of God who have been veiled, if they have given themselves up to corruption, whether publicly by marrying or secretly, be not admitted to penance, unless he to whom they had joined themselves has departed from the world.* --XIV. *That handmaids of God not yet consecrated, if afterwards they have wished to marry, be received to penance.*

[0469A]From the old codices of the collection of Dionysius Exiguus. IX. *That a bishop be not ordained without the knowledge of the metropolitan.* --X. ## 6.

On the other hand, in the Colb., Langob. manuscript and in another, no. 3368, is found *sicut vetus consuetudo exigit*, and the preceding words, *synodus statuit*, etc., are omitted. This reading is favoured by what Innocent writes, whether in Epistle 29, to the Council of Carthage, n. 1: *Keeping the examples of ancient tradition, and mindful of ecclesiastical discipline, you have strengthened with true reason the vigour of our religion no less now in consulting than before when you pronounced, you who have shown your approval that the judgment should be referred to us*; or in Epistle 30, to the Council of Milevis, n. 2: *Diligently and fittingly do you consult the secret counsels of the apostolic honour . . . concerning anxious matters, what judgment is to be held, following, that is, the ancient rule, which you know has always been kept with me throughout the whole world.* The same is supported both by Cyril to Celestine, Epistle 8, n. 1, speaking thus: *The old custom of the Churches urges that matters of this kind be communicated to thy holiness*; and by Leo, Epistle 5, n. 5, where he asks that the greater causes be referred to him *for the tradition of the ancient institution and the reverence owed to the apostolic see*. ## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER.

[0481B]

## 1.

*This letter is shorter in some books, fuller in others. Who cut it down.* --Some books present this letter shorter, others fuller. In the shorter form it was first published by Jacques Merlin, and was then reprinted in the same manner both in the collection of pontifical letters and in various editions of the councils, until Jacques Sermondus, having found it entire in old books, judged that it should be published for the public good. In the exemplars of the Spanish collection, such as the libraries of the Churches of Laon, Noyon and Beauvais preserve, as in all the exemplars of Isidore Mercator, it is had only mutilated. Hence we suspected that it was first truncated by the one who put together the Spanish collection of canons. But that suspicion was then removed by the Colbert codex 408, *On the Institution of Clerics*, written 700 years ago, and another like it and no more recent, the Coislin, which, although they are composed of the monuments of the Spanish collection alone, [0481C] nevertheless retain those chapters of this letter which are lacking in the shorter copy. Finally, when we learned that sound and genuine exemplars of the Spanish collection still exist in the Churches of Urgel, Gerona and Ripoll, in which this letter is read entire, we were fully persuaded that it had been truncated not by him who arranged that collection, but by some other. And since in all the exemplars of Isidore Mercator without exception it is had only mutilated and cut down, who would think another author of this deed should be sought? Nor is it surprising that a man who made no scruple of forging many things, interpolating others, altering more in various ways, did not fear to suppress some things as well. Content, namely, to have copied out Innocent's general decrees, he withdrew the rest, which pertain to special persons or causes, as more foreign to his purpose. Nor do the aforesaid books of Laon, Noyon and Beauvais stand in the way of this opinion. For although [0482A] they were copied from the Spanish collection, yet it is clear, expressly from the letter of Pope Vigilius to Profuturus, that he by whom they were written or dictated also had the collection of Isidore by him, and sometimes, although rarely, preferred it to the Spanish. Further, this letter of Innocent is preserved entire not only in the genuine exemplars of the Spanish collection but also in the very old one of Corbie, and in that of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, now Colbert's. Since these things are so, that nothing remains for the reader to desire, we now present it entire from the fidelity of the sounder codices, in such a way that we also indicate, at its end, how it was published by Mercator.



## 2.

*That it is inscribed to the bishops of the synod of Toledo, not of Toulouse.* --In both kinds of exemplars a false inscription is prefixed to it. And in the preliminary index of the Corbie codex, indeed, it is given this title: *Epistola Innocentii papae ad universos episcopos ecclesiae Tolosanae de universis herisebus* [n: (leg. haeresibus)] *vel de ordinationibus episcoporum, et caetera in epistola requirenda:* [0482B] but at the head of the letter itself this superscription is set before it: *Innocentius episcopis universis in Tolosana synodo constitutis.* The same is read also in the one of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, except that in this one *diversis* has been substituted for *universis*. In most exemplars too, of the Spanish as well as of the Isidorian collection, it is likewise inscribed *universis episcopis in Tolosana synodo constitutis*. Nor did Merlin change this inscription. Indeed Jacques Sirmond also retained the same, and on that account gave this letter a place among the very councils of Gaul. « On which matter, he says in the preliminary *Monitum*, although I understood that it could with good reason be doubted, yet it seemed better that it should stand here entire, even in another's place, especially since it had hitherto been mutilated, than perhaps be missed in its own. » Afterwards, however, he added in the notes that it did not seem doubtful to him « that it was written to the bishops of Spain after the synod of Toledo indeed, but concerning the things done in it, or that followed afterwards. Wherefore, he says, I judge that the ancient inscription of the letter should be restored, [0482C] so that *in Toletana synodo* is read. » Further, he calls it *ancient* because, having already been restored by Crabbe, it was retained by those who reprinted either the councils or the letters of the Roman pontiffs. Before that too it prevailed at least in some manuscripts. We ourselves, among the various codices of Isidore's collection, have come upon one of Navarre written at least 600 years ago, and another of the monastery of St Martin of Champs, which show *in Toletana synodo*. Nor is the soundness of this reading to be doubted, as what we are about to subjoin will confirm. And whence the other crept in may be conjectured from various manuscripts compared with one another.

## 3.

*How it came about that it was inscribed* TO THE SYNOD OF TOULOUSE. --Although in the Noyon exemplar this letter is inscribed *universis episcopis in Tolosana civitate constitutis*, yet in the general index of the same it is headed *ad universos Tolotanos episcopos*. That *Tolotanos* was written there for *Toletanos*, not for *Tolosanos*, is proved by the codex of Saint-Germain, no. 424, [0483A] containing a collection of canons put together 800 years ago, in which, as often as any synod of Toledo is cited, it is constantly called *Tolotana*. Since, therefore, here too the scribes had written *Tolotana* for *Toletana*, the copyists judged the more readily that *Tolosana* ought to be restored, because they both saw a letter of Innocent *ad Exsuperium Tolosanum*, and in the text of this letter, n. 3, read corruptly *Galliarum* or *Galliorum*, in place of *Galliciorum* or *Gallaecorum*. Moreover, since below, n. 6, where from the testimony of the Colbert exemplar we read that Rufinus *in Toletano concilio erroris tui veniam postulasse*, the Corbie one shows *Tolosano* for *Toletano*, no one will fail to agree that the same fault could have crept into the inscription with equal ease.

## 4.

*That it was written to the fathers of the First Council of Toledo.* --What that synod is to which Innocent now writes, and when it was held, is disputed. Baronius, in the earlier edition of the *Annals*, had laid down two things as certain: first, that this letter of Innocent was written to the First Council of Toledo; the other, that this council [0483B] was celebrated in the last consulship of Stilicho, that is, in the year of Christ 405. But in the latest edition he changed his opinion, and, persuaded that the First Council of Toledo is to be dated to the first consulship of Stilicho, and thus to the year of Christ 400, he thought that this letter pertains to some later synod of Toledo. To this opinion many subscribe, and by name Antoine Pagi. And the former opinion, by which the First Council of Toledo was put off to the second consulship of Stilicho, can by no means be defended. But neither does there seem to be any reason why we should distinguish the council, to whose bishops Innocent now writes, from the First of Toledo. That this may become more evident, it will be worth the labour to weigh what has been published under the name of the First Council of Toledo.

## 5.

*The three parts [sic: *patres*] of the First Council of Toledo as published.* --In this council three parts are to be distinguished. The first consists of the preface, 20 canons, and the subscriptions of the bishops. The second contains the rule of faith and [0483C] eighteen chapters against the heresies, with this inscription: *Here begins the rule of the catholic faith against all heresies, and most especially against the Priscillians, which the bishops of Tarragona, Carthagena, Lusitania and Baetica made, and with the precept of Leo, pope of the city of Rome, transmitted to Balconius, bishop of Gallicia.* The last is marked with this title: *Here begin the exemplars of the professions in the council of Toledo against the sect of Priscillian, era* 438. Then follows the preface: « After the council was held on the Kalends of September, on the third day before the Nones of September, after various hearings then held, on the eighth day before the Ides of September there were excerpted from the full acts the professions of the lord Symphosius and the lord Dictinius, bishops of holy memory, and of the lord Comasius of holy memory, then a presbyter, which among the rest they made in the council of Toledo concerning the condemnation of Priscillian or of his sect, in this manner: After some things, and among some things done at the same time, Bishop Dictinius said, » etc., that is, the rest [0483D] of Dictinius's profession, after which, set down, is subjoined the profession of Comasius, with this preface or interlocution placed first: « In the era as above, on the third day before the Ides of September, the professions of the lord Simphosius and the lord Dictinius, bishops of holy memory, and of Comasius of holy memory, then a presbyter. Comasius said. » Finally this profession of Comasius is followed by « the exemplar of the definitive sentence, transferred from the acts. On the day as above the bishops said: Let the sentence be read. And he read, » etc.

## 6.

*They present a council celebrated in the year 447.* --But how those three parts cohere among themselves, or can be referred to one and the same council, no one, as far as I know, has hitherto explained. Only this is agreed among the learned, that the middle part belongs to that council which Leo, writing to Turibius in the year 447, commanded to be gathered; and thus that it is foreign to the First Council of Toledo. Hence, after Baronius, Binius notes that it was inserted among the other two *by the error of the collector*. But neither can the last [0484A] be more fittingly referred to the First Council of Toledo. For the bishops who speak in it indicate that they are holding a synod when Symphosius, Dictinius and Comasius were already dead, who, it is agreed, were still living at the time of the First Council of Toledo, and indeed, present at that very council, condemned the heresy of Priscillian. But those three parts will cohere with one another most aptly if they are referred to the general council of the Spains which was gathered by order of Pope Leo: so that in it first the 20 canons of the First Council of Toledo were read out and confirmed, then the rule of faith was composed, 18 new canons were added, and lastly some excerpts from the full acts of the First Synod of Toledo were recited. What therefore has been published as the First Council of Toledo would more aptly be inscribed: *The council of the Spains which the bishops of Tarragona, Carthagena, Lusitania and Baetica celebrated by the precept of Leo, in the year 447, on the Kalends of September: to which are prefixed the 20 canons of the First Council of Toledo, celebrated in the year 400, and certain excerpts of the same council, copied from [0484B] its full acts, are subjoined.*



## 7.

*That a council was held at Toledo in the year 400.* -- But we have so restored that council to the year 447 as not to deny that another was held at Toledo in the year 400, but rather to assert it plainly from that very fact. Of this council of Toledo Idatius speaks thus in his *Chronicle*, at the year 400: « In the province of Carthagena, in the city of Toledo, a synod of bishops is gathered, in which, as is contained in the acts, Symphosius and Dictinius and other bishops of the province of Gallaecia with them, followers of Priscillian, condemn his most blasphemous heresy, together with its very author, by the subscription of their profession. Certain things also are laid down to be observed concerning the discipline of the Church, Bishop Ortygius, who had been ordained at Celenae, taking part in the same council. » Now the council held by the order of Leo in the year 447 first reviews the canons pertaining to discipline which the synod of Toledo issued *Stilichone consule*, that is, in the year 400: and afterwards, from the [0484C] acts of the same synod, dated according to Spanish custom *era* 438, for the year 400, it presents not only the professions of Symphosius, Dictinius and others condemning the heresy of Priscillian together with its author himself, but also the sentence of the same council, by which their honour is preserved to them, and which is closed, in Ortygius's favour, with these words: « But to our brother Ortygius we pronounce that the churches from which he had been driven are to be restored. » Whence the agreement of those acts with the *Chronicle* of Idatius is manifest. Moreover, in the sentence of the synod of Toledo just mentioned Simplician is recorded as the one who then ruled the Church of Milan. But Simplician succeeded Ambrose only in the year 397, and he himself, before the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July of the year 401, had Venerius as successor, as is clear from the Council of Carthage inserted in the *Codex canonum Ecclesiae Africanae*, c. 56. And hence, therefore, the time at which the synod of Toledo was celebrated is confirmed.

## 8.

*In what sense the following [0484D] letter can be said to have been written to this synod.* --These things being laid down, since it is ascertained and beyond doubt that that synod of Toledo, whose canons and acts are reported in the aforesaid council of the Spains, was celebrated in the year 400, no controversy now seems to remain but that the following letter of Innocent was inscribed to this synod of Toledo. For first, in it, as may be read at nos. 6 and 7, the acts and decrees of this synod are praised more than once. Next, Innocent, at no. 10, notes that he is addressing the bishops « who decreed by their sentence that ordinations are to be made according to the Nicene rules. » And indeed the prelates of the First Council of Toledo, when in the very preface they had decreed « that the constitutions of the Nicene council are first of all to be kept in perpetuity, and that there must be no departing from them », proceed to lay down what ought to be observed in ordinations. Not, however, that Innocent is to be understood as writing to the synod of Toledo as though still assembled, but rather to those bishops who had come together in it. Unless one prefer [0485A] that here by the name *of the synod of Toledo* the bishops belonging to the synod of Toledo are understood. Certainly the praised pope speaks of the First Council of Toledo, no. 6, as celebrated *long since*. Nor does that *Patruinus of venerable memory*, in whose place he records, no. 9, that Gregory was substituted, seem other than the one who is read to have subscribed first to the canons of the First Council of Toledo. Finally, Innocent's zeal in this letter aims chiefly at this, that he may suppress and settle the schism which arose from Symphosius, Dictinius and others having been received with their honours at the synod of Toledo, and which was spreading more widely day by day. Wherefore it is manifest that some interval came between this letter and that synod. But how much came between cannot be defined with certainty. We may only conjecture that this letter was written before Spain was thrown into disorder by the tumults of war, and thus before the year 408, in which Constantine snatched that province from Honorius. But whether the letter is later than the preceding one or not, although we do not know, yet on account of the affinity of the matters defined in both concerning the ordinations of clerics, [0485B] it will be pleasing and convenient to the reader to have both next to one another. Nor is it now of much concern to him to have ascertained the time at which it was written, since he holds to whom, on what occasion, and with what design it was written. Here perhaps someone will wonder how the same pontiff now so earnestly praises and approves the indulgence of the synod of Toledo towards the followers of Priscillian, who afterwards so constantly refused that clerics ordained by Bonosus should keep their honours. But a wise priest ought to discern between leprosy and leprosy, and to search out when the severity of discipline is either to be retained or relaxed. For although the holy leaders of the churches are animated by the same spirit, yet at different times they have laid down different things concerning clerics returning to the Church from heresy or schism. The Nicene fathers, can. 8, willed the Novatians to remain in the clergy. On the testimony of the Africans, a council beyond the sea, in the times of Siricius and Ambrose, forbade that clerics coming from heresy [0485C] should keep their honours. But the Council of Toledo, in the year 400, judged that this was to be granted to the followers of Priscillian, and Innocent now approves its sentence *for the purpose of unity*, who in the year 414 will sharply vindicate the severity of ecclesiastical discipline in the case of the Bonosians. The Council of Carthage, however, held in the year 401, judged that this moderation should be used: that for clerics returning, where by their return some compensation of unity is made, their honours should be preserved, and where there is no compensation of this kind, they should be refused [n: (Cod. can. eccl. Afr., c. 68)].

## EPISTLE III. On [nt: We have borrowed this title and those that follow from Sirmond, not from the manuscripts.] the dissension and corrupted discipline of the Churches of Spain.



## I.

*That some bishops wrongly dissent from others on account of converts received from heresy.* --II. *On bishops [0486A] ordained by Rufinus and Minicius in other men's churches against the canons.* --III. *That the cause of Bishop John be examined, and of the others who were shunning the fellowship of communion.* --IV. *On the faulty ordinations of many, that what has been usurped hitherto be so passed over that it be forbidden for the future.* --V. *That the complaint of Gregory, bishop of Merida, be examined.* --VI. *Whom it is lawful to admit to the order of the clergy: and of what sort they are to be who are chosen. And that she too makes a man a bigamist who was his wife before baptism.*

*INNOCENT to all the bishops assembled in the synod of Toledo, most beloved brethren, greeting in the Lord.*

## 1.

*A schism in Spain. And contempt of the canons.* -- Though an excessive care has often held me anxious concerning [nt: Already before the First Council of Toledo a certain dissension had prevailed among the Spaniards concerning the ordinations of clerics. Wherefore Bishop Patruinus, in the preface of this council, speaks first thus: *Since we have each begun to do different things in our churches, and from this there are such great scandals, which reach even to schism, if it please you, let us decree by common counsel what is to be followed by all the bishops in ordaining clerics.* But after the council just mentioned, to this cause of schism was added another, when some admitted, and others contended should be rejected, those converted from the heresy of Priscillian to catholic communion whom the same synod had received in their honours. Innocent now tries to heal that twofold cause of so great an evil.] [0486B] the dissension and schism of the Churches, which report declares to be creeping more widely day by day through the Spains, and to be advancing at a quicker pace, the necessary time has come in which so great an amendment could not be put off, and a fitting medicine ought to be provided. For our brethren, our fellow bishop [nt: Among those who subscribed the First Council of Toledo, Hilarius is read in the fourth place.] Hilarius and the presbyter Elpidius, partly moved by love of unity, partly roused, as was fitting, by the ruin with which the province labours, have come to the apostolic see, and with grief and groaning have set forth that in the very bosom of the faith the peace within the province has been violated, the order of discipline confounded, and many things committed against the canons of the fathers, order being despised and the rules neglected, in the usurpation of churches, and that the concord in which the whole stability of our faith consists cannot be retained: which things [0486C] are kept in the record of acts drawn up in the session [nt: That is, of the Roman clergy, this name being taken from the more worthy rank. To the same session, above all in causes of this kind, the bishops who were staying at Rome were also accustomed to be summoned.] of the presbytery, and can be shown to you by reading.

## CHAP. I.



## 2.

*The bishops of Baetica separate themselves from the rest on account of the Gallaecians who were received.* --First, then, as regards the faith itself, a dissension has arisen because the bishops of Baetica or of Carthagena, on account of communion with the Gallicians, have withdrawn [nt: So the Corb. and Colb. manuscripts. But in Sirmond, *dissederunt*. *Discesserunt* would rather have to be restored. Earlier, in the Corb. manuscript, *Galliarum*; in the Colb., *Galliorum*; perhaps in place of *Gallicorum* or *Gallaeorum*. For, as we heard above from the *Chronicle* of Idatius, the bishops of Gallaecia were Symphosius, Dictinius and others, who at the synod of Toledo condemned the heresy of Priscillian, together with its very author, by their subscription; that the Baetici and Carthaginians took ill their being received into peace, and therefore fell away from the communion of the rest, is not at all surprising. Gregory, bishop of Elvira in the province of Baetica, had sown deep the seeds of the Luciferian error. Nor is it astonishing that they propagated an unhappy fruit down to the times of Innocent.] from the peace of all: which is not only not diminished, but is even increased day by day by the zeal of contention, since, each one purposing to obtain what he wished, they have made out of such animosity an eternal round of evil and a kind of circle: when surely for every good man it is better in matters of this kind to be overcome than by an evil habit to obtain a perverse [0487A] purpose which has once pleased him. For what other cause, in former times too, was there of that Lucifer, besides obstinacy, which drew him back from concord [nt: In the manuscripts, *cum illorum*. For when, for the purpose of unity, [nt: The Colb. manuscript: *Symposius*. That Symposius is not to be believed the one who subscribed the synod of Saragossa held against the Priscillianists in the year 380. The fathers of Toledo continue: *But let Symphosius, an aged religious man, who did what we have written above, remain in his church . . . thence* (that is, from the pope and from the bishop of Milan) *he will await communion, whence he had before received the hope of future peace. Which we have decreed is to be observed also for Dictinius and Anterius.* Then there follows next: *But we have laid down that, before communion is restored to them through the pope* (see again the name of pope for the Roman pontiff) *or through St Simplician, neither bishops nor presbyters nor deacons are to be ordained by them.* Why do they pass sentence on all those bishops in such a way as to wish it to be awaited until communion is restored to the same by letters of the apostolic see and of the bishop of Milan? Light is thrown on this question by similar decrees both of the Council of Carthage held in the year 401, on the 18th day of June, and of another celebrated in the same year on the 13th day of September, by which, as may be seen in the *Codex canonum Ecclesiae Africanae*, c. 65, the Africans resolve that it should be sent to Anastasius the Roman pontiff and to Venerius bishop of Milan, that it might be lawful for them through these both to promote to the clergy infants baptized by the Donatists, and to receive in their honours clerics who wished to pass over from the Donatists to catholic unity, where this seemed to profit Christian peace. For they subjoin the reason of this matter, *because this had been forbidden from these sees*. Nor do the fathers of Toledo teach obscurely that they had determined that the aforesaid bishops should await the communion of the Roman and Milanese prelates for this reason, that some kind of judgment concerning them too had already gone before from those sees, inasmuch as Ambrose and Siricius had prescribed to them by letters certain conditions of peace. Whence the sentence of the Spaniards concerning Vegetinus is more absolute, in this manner: *But Vegetinus, against whom no sentence had been specially pronounced before, having given the profession which the synod accepted, we decree is to be restored to our communion.*] Symphosius himself also and [nt: That Dictinius had not only followed the tenets of Priscillian, but had also asserted them in books. Afterwards, however, in the Council of Toledo, detesting whatever he had either thought or written amiss, he said: *All my presumption in my writings I censure and condemn.* And soon after: *Again I repeat, whatever I wrote in my former comprehension and in the beginnings of my conversion, I reject all with my whole heart. . . . Except the name of God, I anathematize all . . . All things that are found against the faith I condemn together with their very author.* Yet his writings could not be suppressed so carefully but that down to the times of Pope Leo they were read by many with veneration, to whom indeed that pope, Epistle 17, n. 19, counsels that *they ought rather to love his restoration than his fall*.] Dictinius, condemning the depraved heresy, were received, so that, such persons being cut off, the inbred dissension might be utterly extinguished; there were found some to whom the very correction rightly made [n: (Mss. facit)] was displeasing. And now [0487B] the churches are at variance, which with no small animosity dissemble from one another ( *Or* disagree and go off into enmities). But if the correction had been kept by the priests with sounder counsel, both the state of the catholic faith would [0488A] have remained entire, and no scandal would have corrupted the concord useful in all things.



## 3.

*That some bear with an unjust mind the honours kept for them.* --For I ask why they should have grieved that Symphosius and Dictinius, and the others who condemned the detestable heresy, were then received into the catholic faith? Is it [nt: Sirmond, with the Corc. and Colb. manuscripts: *Numquidnam aliquid*. The codex of Bonneval: *Num quod non aliquid*. By recalling *num* from the first two and *quod non* from the last, the reading is now had entire and clear. The very examples by which Innocent now proves that clerics may lawfully have their honours kept for them after penance, Augustine too employs for the same cause, Epistle 185, n. 45: *For holy David also*, he says, *did penance for deadly crimes, and yet he remained in his honour: and blessed Peter, when he shed most bitter tears, certainly repented of having denied the Lord, and yet he remained an apostle.*] that they did not lose anything of the honours which they held? But if this pricks or goads any, let them read that Peter the apostle was, after his tears, what he had been; let them consider that Thomas, after that doubting of his, lost nothing of his former merits; and finally that David, the eminent prophet, after his open confession, was not deprived of the merits of his prophecy. But if the amendment of conversion both cuts off the errors themselves and retains the dignities; what evil reason [0488B] is it, out of a purpose of obstinacy, to be unwilling to hold to the way of right and the road which leads to salvation?

## 4.

*The force of unity, and the ruin of schism.* --Wherefore your charity must apply itself, and good priests [0489A] must strive, that, with teaching going before [nt: By which, namely, both the perversity of schism or heresy and the rightness of the catholic faith may be proved, *so that the light of truth may drive out the darkness of error*, says Augustine, Epistle 93, n. 5, *and the Church may be seen to receive men corrected rather than perverse*.], all who have been scattered may be gathered into the unity of the catholic faith; and there may begin to be one impregnable body, which, if it be separated into parts, will lie open to every injury of laceration, and will suffer an internal plague from itself, when the frame itself fights against itself. But let all the priests receive these things, written in general concerning the restoration of unity, as though written to each. Thereafter let your charity turn its mind in detail to all the things which shall be proposed.

## CHAP. II.



## 5.

*Rufinus and Minicius usurped ordinations in other men's churches.* --For it could not lie hidden that Rufinus and Minicius, bishops, usurped the ordaining of bishops in other men's churches, against the Nicene canons. That [n: (Nicaen. can. 4, 6 et 16)] no one [0489B] may dare to claim this for himself, provision must now at least be made by us wholesomely: lest the dissimulation by improper [nt: It would be said more clearly: *ne improba usurpatio dissimulatione*.] usurpation grow stronger for the worse, and a rule be made of custom which does not come from the very discipline that has been committed to writing. In which matter let the complaint of Hilary, our brother and fellow priest, be heard first, who asserted that Rufinus had been engaged with every kind of assault against the peace of the churches, and had some while ago asked pardon for his error in the council [nt: So the Colb. manuscript, where the Corb. has *Tholosano*. Here it must be recalled that the acts of the synod of Toledo have by no means come down to us full and entire, but only fragments of them, recited in a later council as then suited the purpose; and that nothing was recited in that council except what concerned the Priscillianists. Rufinus, however, was rather one of those bishops of whom Patruinus complains in the preface of the first council of Toledo, namely those who, having undertaken illegitimate ordinations, stirred up such scandals as went as far as schism, not one of those who had been devoted to Priscillian. The same is to be thought of Minicius also. Whence also that part of the acts of the council of Toledo which concerned them was passed over in the aforesaid council.] of Toledo, and now, although the prerogative of ordaining [nt: Sirmond and Labbe: *sacerdotis*. More correctly the manuscripts: *sacerdotes*. ## CHAP. III.



## 6.

*That John be cut off, if he does not cease to resist the decree on receiving those who return to the Church, to which he had subscribed.* --Concerning JOHN also, the bishop, whose consent was given through legates in the synod of Toledo to the reception of SYMPHOSIUS and DICTINIUS, and to whom that correction seemed approvable, let the things which followed afterwards be examined. ## CHAP. IV.



## 7.

*Certain ordinations against the canons to be tolerated for the sake of peace. ## CHAP. V.



## 8.

*That the complaint of Gregory of Merida be heard.* --Of GREGORY also, bishop of Merida, who was ordained in the place of PATRUINUS [nt: Those who judged that Patruinus, whose name is read in the preface of the first council of Toledo, and who subscribed first to it, was bishop of Toledo, are corrected at this place. ## CHAP. VI.



## 9.

*That the Nicene rules be kept in ordinations [0492A]. ## CHAP. II.



## 5.

And this was asked, what ought to be observed concerning those who, having been given over at every time after baptism to the pleasures of incontinence, at the extreme end of their life ask at once for penance and for the reconciliation of communion [n: (23, q. 4, c. 45)].

## 6.

Concerning these the earlier observance was harsher; the later, mercy intervening, more inclined to mildness. For the earlier custom held that penance be granted, but communion denied. For since in those times persecutions were frequent, lest the facility of communion, once granted, should not recall men, secure of reconciliation, from lapsing, communion was rightly denied; penance was granted, lest all be wholly denied: and the reason of the time made the remission harsher. But after our Lord [0498C] restored peace to his Churches, the terror being now driven off, it was decided that communion be given to those departing [nt: So Labbe, Sirmond and several and better manuscripts. Other printed editions, however: *obeuntibus*; and below, with Dionysius and the Isidorian collection, *subsequi* for *sequi*. That harsher discipline, recalled by Innocent, prevails chiefly in the council of Elvira, can. 6, 7, 8, etc. It had prevailed before in Africa also, but only among certain bishops, who indeed did not think peace should be given to adulterers in such a way, and shut the place of penance against adulteries altogether, and yet did not withdraw from the college of their fellow bishops who thought otherwise and granted them peace, as Cyprian relates, Epistle 52, to Antonianus. There is besides a certain example of this severity in the common book of Ambrose on the Fall of a consecrated virgin, to whom, c. 8, n. 58, this speech is addressed: *Cling to penance until the end of life, and do not presume that pardon is given thee by a human day; for he deceives thee who would promise thee this. For since thou hast sinned properly against the Lord, it befits thee to await the remedy from him alone in the day of judgment.* And although Cyprian, in the letter cited, proves at length that neither penance nor indulgence is to be denied to the lapsed; yet toward its end he decrees this: *Those not doing penance, nor testifying the grief of their offences with their whole heart and with a manifest profession of their lamentation, we have judged are to be wholly kept from the hope of communion and peace, if in sickness and in danger they have begun to beg: because it is not repentance for the offence but the warning of impending death that drives them to ask; nor is he worthy to receive comfort in death who did not think that he was to die.* Which sentence indeed, if with Pamelius it is to be judged somewhat harsher, the same will have to be said also of this canon 22 of the first synod of Arles: *Concerning those who apostatize and never present themselves at the church, nor even seek to do penance, and afterwards, seized by sickness, ask for communion, it has pleased that communion is not to be given them, unless they recover and bring forth worthy fruits of penance.* But this so seemed good to them, not because they greatly distrusted the clemency of God, but the truth of penance of this kind. And indeed Cyprian, toward the end of the book to Demetrianus, teaches that no penance is late for one still remaining in this world, and that no one ought to be deterred from it either by sins or by years; that pardon is given to him who confesses, and that one passes to immortality under death itself. Which, although he says it chiefly of the grace of baptism, there is yet no doubt that he thinks the same of every penance undertaken after baptism, provided it be true. Hence, as is to be seen in his Epistles 13, 14, 15, etc., he always took great care that there should not be lacking one who would impart peace and communion to the lapsed, after the exomologesis had been made, if they had begun to be pressed by some sickness and danger. What Innocent now defines, Celestine afterwards, Epistle 4, to the bishops of the province of Vienne and Narbonne, n. 3, and Leo, Epistle 100, to Theodore, n. 5, expressly confirm, and before them the Roman clergy, in Cyprian, Epistle 3, to the clergy of Carthage, had prescribed in these words: *If those who have fallen into this temptation begin to be seized by sickness, and do penance for their deed, and desire communion, they certainly ought to be helped.* Jerome, above, p. 550, notes that the example of the thief was set before us, lest anyone should at any time think conversion late. But there he asks for conversion and change.], [0499A] both on account of the mercy of the Lord, as a viaticum for those setting out, and lest we seem to follow the harshness and severity of the Novatian heretic who denies pardon. Communion therefore shall be granted, with penance, at the last: so that men of this kind, even at their very end, by the permission of our Saviour, may be delivered from perpetual destruction.

## 8.

Concerning these we read nothing defined by the elders. Concerning these, therefore, we hold thus, as has been observed hitherto, lest we should seem either to overturn discipline or to come against the authority of the Lord. ## CHAP. IV.



## 9.

And this was desired to be known, why husbands who communicate do not come together with adulterous wives, when on the contrary wives are seen to remain in the fellowship of adulterous husbands.

## 10.

Concerning this [n: (32, q. 6, c. 23; Ivo p. 8, c. 214)] the Christian religion condemns adultery in both sexes with equal reason. But women do not easily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden [0500A] sins do not have punishment. Husbands, however, have been accustomed more freely to report adulterous wives before the priests: and therefore to the women, their crime being disclosed, communion is denied. But of the husbands, the offence lying hidden, no one is easily kept away on suspicions. Who certainly will be removed, if his shameful deed be detected. Since then the cause is equal, sometimes, when proof is lacking, the reason for punishment is at rest.
