## 2.

I rejoice therefore, dearest brethren, that you have sent a letter to us by our brother and fellow bishop Julius: and that, while you take care of the churches over which you preside, you show your solicitude for the benefit of all: and that you ask that something be decreed which may profit all alike throughout all the churches of the whole world: so that the Church, established by her own rules [0583C], [nt: The Roman edition and the more recent Councils have *ex hoc*, and then, with the older ones, *quod illos caveat pronuntiationis justae firmata decretalibus* (Merlin: *petere*; Crabbe: *patere*; the Roman edition and those following: *pavere*) *non possit*. Garnier, cutting out *hoc quod illos caveat*, kept *et pronuntiationis justae firmata decretalibus pavere non possit*. Our reading is that of Quesnel, the Augustine edition and the better manuscripts, except that in Quesnel *hoc* has been struck out, and in the Augustine edition, as in the Corbie and Saint-Germain manuscripts, *parete* stands in place of *patere*. It is then to be understood thus, as if Innocent said: You ask that it be decreed by me that the Church, already established by her ancient rules, being now also strengthened by this new decree justly pronounced, by which she is bidden to beware of those heretics mentioned, may not henceforth lie open to such men, but may remain shut off from them for ever.] strengthened also by this decree of just pronouncement, by which she may beware of them, may not lie open to such men as, instructed, nay rather destroyed, by perverse subtleties [0584A] of words, disputing under the appearance of the catholic faith, as if breathing out a pestilential poison, so as to corrupt towards the worse part the hearts of men who think rightly, seek to overturn the whole discipline of true doctrine. It must therefore be healed the more speedily, lest an accursed [nt: One of the Colbert manuscripts: *exsecrandis animorum moribus inserpat*. The other: *exsecrandos animis morbos inserpat*. The Roman edition and the Councils, with some other manuscripts, keep the word *inserpat*. In its place the Saint-Germain and Corbie manuscripts better show *inrepat*.] disease creep further into souls: just as a physician, when he sees some sickness in this earthly body, reckons it a great proof of his art if someone despaired of quickly escapes through his intervention; or when he has looked upon a putrid wound, applies poultices, or the other things by which the wound that had arisen may be closed over; and if, remaining, it cannot be healed, lest it corrupt the rest of the body with its decay, he cuts off with the knife what was doing harm, so as to keep the rest whole and untouched. That must therefore be cut off [0584B] which has crept upon the body, all too pure and sound, like a wound; lest, when it is cleansed too slowly, a bilge of this evil that cannot afterwards be drained should settle almost in the very vitals.

## 3.

For what are we henceforth to reckon right in their minds concerning these men, who think that they owe it to themselves that they are good, and do not consider him whose grace they obtain daily? But now these men, who are such, obtain no grace of God; [nt: Crabbe, and after him the editions of the Councils and the Roman: *quia sine illo*.] who trust that they can attain without him as much as those who ask of him scarcely [nt: The Roman edition and the Councils, with the Pithou and Isidorian manuscripts: *et accipiunt*. One Colbert codex: *ut accipiunt*; whence Quesnel preferred *ut accipiant*. In the Augustine edition, as in the Corbie manuscript: *accipere*, the particle *et* not being put before it, which is kept with the Saint-Germain and others. The sentence will be clear if arranged in this way: *quantum vix illi etiam, qui postulant, accipere promerentur*.] also merit to receive. For what can be so unjust, so barbarous, so ignorant of all religion, so hostile to Christian minds, as to deny that thou owest whatever thou obtainest in daily grace to him to whom thou thyself confessest that thou [0584C] owest that thou wast born? Wilt thou then be more excellent for thyself in providing, than [nt: So the manuscripts. But the Roman edition and the Councils: *quam potest is esse*.] can be in him who brought it about that thou shouldst be? [nt: Garnier: *Si huic putes debere*. Other printed editions: *Et cum te putes ei debere*. Pelagius is here refuted without being named: who, distinguishing to be able, to will and to be, placed being able in nature, willing in choice, and being in effect. Then he so granted that being able belongs properly to God, the author of nature, as to contend that willing and being, or acting, are to be referred to man. He taught that it is of God alone that man is able to will and to accomplish the good; but that he wills to accomplish it, and actually accomplishes it, and so too that he wills to be good and perfect, or even is so, he proclaimed to be of man himself. He did not deny that man is always helped by the aid of grace: but he placed that aid in this, that God never fails to give the possibility of willing and of working. See his very words in Augustine, book *On the Grace of Christ*, cap. 4.] And to whom thou thinkest thou owest that thou livest, [0585A] how dost thou not think thou owest to him that, by obtaining his daily grace, thou livest thus? And thou who deniest that we need the divine help, as if we [nt: In the Roman edition and the Councils *simus* is missing.] were entirely perfect from our own possibility, how do we not call forth his help [nt: The word *ejus* is recalled from the Saint-Germain manuscript and the Augustine edition. Garnier alone presents this passage thus: *Dic quomodo vere adjutorium ejus in nos, cum tales a nobis etiam esse possimus, provocemus. Eum qui adjutorium Dei negat, rursus vellem interrogare cur dicat nos id non promereri?*] upon us, when we can be such even of ourselves?

## 4.

For I should like to ask him who denies the help of God what he says: that we do not deserve it, or that he cannot bestow it, or that there is nothing on account of which each one ought [nt: Quesnel, with one Colbert manuscript: *praestolari*.] to ask for it? That God is able to do this, his works themselves testify. And that we need daily help, we cannot deny. For whether we live well, [nt: So the manuscripts, and also the old editions of the Councils. But the Roman edition and the more recent Councils, with Garnier: *precamur*.] we call it forth, that we may live better and more holily; or whether, thinking wrongly, we are turned away from good things, we need his aid the more, that we may return to the right way. [0585B] For what should seem so deadly, so headlong towards a fall, so exposed to all dangers, as if, thinking that this alone can suffice us, that we received free choice when we were born, we should seek nothing further from the Lord, that is, forgetful of our author, should abjure his power in order to show ourselves free; as though he who made thee free at thy birth had nothing more that he could give: not knowing that unless grace, implored with great prayers, descends [nt: Garnier: *nequidquam*; and below, *David inclamat*, for *Nam si ille clamat*.] upon us, we should by no means strive to overcome the errors of earthly defilement and of the worldly body, since not free choice, but the aid of God alone, can make us equal to resisting?

## 5.

For if he cries out that he has need of the divine help, who would not worthily have sought it, if free [0585C] choice were of more profit to anyone; since, although a blessed man and already chosen by the Lord, he lacked nothing, yet he so beseeches God, asking: *Be thou my helper, forsake me not, neither despise me, O God my saviour [n: (Psal. XXVI, 9)]*: we ask free choice for ourselves, he [0586A] asks God for himself as helper; we say that what we were born with can suffice us, he prays God that he be not forsaken. [nt: The Roman edition: *Nos ergo dicimus manifeste*, etc. Garnier: *Nos dicimus manifeste, ut quid oremus Deum, ille*: and below, *David ergo*, for *David enim*.] Do we not, I ask, learn plainly what we should pray for, when that man, so greatly blessed, as we said above, longs not to be despised? For those who confirm the one must needs refute the other. For let David be accused of being ignorant of prayer and unaware of his own nature, who, though he knows that so much is present in [nt: The Roman edition and the Councils: *in sua natura esse*. Next, Garnier: *adjutorem invocat, nec illi sufficit assiduum invocare*: against the other books, from which it is clear that the word *adjutorem* is governed by the verb *exoptat*.] his nature, longs for God as his helper, and a constant helper, nor does constant suffice him, but, bowed down in prayers, longs that he may never despise him; and throughout the whole body of the psalter he both proclaims and cries this. If then he, so great [nt: Some manuscripts with Quesnel, and also the Roman edition and the Councils: *ita magnum scit, ut assidue diceret*. In the Augustine edition: *ita magnus sicut assidue dicere*. Garnier: *hoc illi tam magnum visum sit, ut assidue diceret, tam necessarium confessum sit*. We keep what the more numerous and older manuscripts present. We should prefer, however, *ita magnus scivit assidue dicere, et ita*.], knows so to say this continually, so confessed it necessary as to teach it: how do Pelagius and Coelestius, setting aside every answer [0586B] of the psalms and renouncing such teaching, trust that they will persuade some that we neither ought to seek the help of God nor need it; when all the saints testify that they can do nothing without it?

## 6.

For that man once, having undergone free [nt: Merlin, and from him Quesnel: *Libero enim arbitrio olim ille perversus*; against all the manuscripts and the other printed editions, not only here, but also in book II of Augustine to Boniface, cap. 4, n. 6, in Prosper's book against the Collator, c. 5, n. 15, and in the epistle of Celestine 21, n. 5, where these same words are cited. Certainly the sense of Innocent calls for *permissus* rather than *perversus*.] choice, while he used his goods too unadvisedly, falling, was sunk into the depths of transgression, and found no way by which he could rise from there; and, deceived for ever by his own liberty, he would have lain under the crushing of this ruin [nt: In the manuscripts, as in the editions of Merlin and the Roman: *ruinae latuisset oppressus* or *oppressum*, except that in the Pithou *oppressu* stands, and in the Corbie *jacuisset* has been restored by an ancient hand: an emendation proved right both by Augustine's book II to Boniface against the two letters of the Pelagians, n. 6, and by the epistle 21 of Pope Celestine, cap. 4, where these words are cited. Although in those two places too manuscripts are not lacking which present *latuisset oppressu*. In Crabbe, and thence in the editions of the Councils, one may read here *huic ruinae suae jacuisset oppressus*; in Garnier and Quesnel, *hujus ruina subjacuisset oppressus*.], had not the coming of Christ afterwards [nt: So the manuscripts with great agreement, together with the Augustine edition. But in the printed editions: *per suam gratiam*.] raised him up for his grace: who through the purification of the new regeneration cleansed all past fault by the laver of his baptism; and, strengthening his state, so that he might proceed more rightly and more steadily, yet did not deny his grace for the time to come. For although he had redeemed [0586C] man from past sins, yet knowing that he could sin again, he kept in reserve for himself many things for his restoration, by which he could correct him even after these things: he supplies daily remedies, and unless we strive relying and trusting on them, we shall by no means be able to overcome [0587A] human errors. For it is necessary that, as we conquer when he helps, so, when he does not help, we be conquered again.

## 7.

But I could say more, were it not evident that you have said everything. Whoever therefore is seen to assent to this opinion, by which he would say that we have no need of the divine help, professes himself an enemy of the catholic faith and ungrateful for the benefits of God. [nt: The conjunction *Nam* is recalled from the editions of Merlin, Crabbe, the Augustine edition and most manuscripts. Then in the Isidorian manuscripts *nostra* is missing. Next the Roman edition and the Councils, with some manuscripts: *Sic enim*, where with the other books we prefer *Ipsi enim*. But Garnier, judging this passage mutilated, advises by a note written in the margin that it could be repaired thus: *Pelagium igitur et Coelestium, quos auctores nefarii prorsus et omnibus anathematizandi erroris advertistis, justa sententia damnastis: nec illi nostra*, etc. But these words of theirs at the end of the preceding epistle 26 do not sound like a sentence pronounced by name against Pelagius and Coelestius by the fathers of the council of Carthage: *If Pelagius and Coelestius have been corrected, or say that they never held these things, and deny that whatever writings have been brought forward against them are theirs, and there is no way in which they may be convicted of lying, yet let whoever shall have been found a champion of the doctrines whose authors they are thought to be be anathema in general terms.* Nothing appears in this passage of Innocent either, from which it should be judged *matilus*.] For neither are they worthy of our communion, which they have polluted by preaching in such a way. For they themselves of their own accord, while they follow those things which they say, have fled further from the true religion. For since the whole of this consists in our profession, and in our daily prayers we do nothing but seek how we may obtain the mercy of God; how can we bear these men boasting? What error, [0587C] I ask, so great blinds their hearts, that if they themselves feel no grace of God, because they are neither worthy nor deserve it, they do not even consider concerning others what divine grace bestows daily on each? They are indeed [nt: So in Garnier and the Augustine edition, as in the better manuscripts. But in other books: *omnes*; and below, *Negantes enim Dei adjutorium*.] most worthy of all blindness, who have not left even this to themselves, that they should believe that they can be recalled from their errors by the divine aid. For denying help, they have taken this away utterly not from others but from themselves: they are to be torn further away and removed far from the vitals of the Church; lest [nt: The printed editions, except the Augustine edition: *ne diu multa*. More fittingly in the Augustine edition, as in the Corbie and Saint-Germain manuscripts: *ne diu inultus multa*. Hence there is aptly joined on: *Si enim diu fuerint sub hac IMPUNITATE*.] the error, long unpunished, seizing on many things, should afterwards grow incurable. For if they have long lived under this impunity, they must needs lead many into this depravity of their mind, and deceive the innocent, or rather the unwary, who follow the catholic [nt: This reading of Garnier, which is also that of the Corbie and Saint-Germain manuscripts, Quesnel approves, although he himself keeps the common one in the Roman edition and the Councils, namely *non sequuntur*. But here in the Augustine edition the particle *nunc* has dropped out by the copyist's drowsiness.] faith now. For they will think that those think rightly [0587C] whom they see still remaining in the Church. Let the unsound wound then be separated from the sound body, and, the breath of the raging disease being removed, let the things that are sincere endure more safely, and let the purer flock be cleansed from this contagion of the evil beast. Let there be an unimpaired perfection of the whole body, which we have learned that you follow and hold by this pronouncement against them, and which we preserve together with you with equal assent. [0588A]

## 8.

Yet if they call forth in themselves some [nt: In the Roman edition and the Councils: *aliquando in se*.] help of God, which up to now they have denied, and recognize that they need his aid, so that they may be freed from this stain into which they had fallen by the crookedness of their heart; and, as if drawn into the light out of a foul darkness, all things being removed and renounced by which their whole sight, lest it should behold [nt: In Quesnel and the Augustine edition: *aspicerent*.] the truth, was befouled and darkened, let them condemn these things which up to now they have held; and at length, applying their mind to right disputations, corrected in some small measure from this stain, they give and submit themselves to be healed [nt: In Garnier: *conciliis*. The preceding word, *sanandos*, which Quesnel removed, all our manuscripts preserve.] by true counsels: if they do this, it will be in the power of the bishops to come to their aid in some degree, and to afford such wounds some care, which the Church is not wont to deny to the lapsed when they have come to their senses: so that, [nt: The word *revocati* is missing in Merlin. In its place the Roman edition and the later Councils have substituted *remoti*.] recalled [0588C] from their precipices, they may be brought back within the sheepfold of the Lord: lest, set outside, and shut out from so great a protection [nt: Quesnel: *praesidio aede munitionis*. Garnier: *praesidio fidae munitionis*. This last reading displeases less.] of the defence of faith, they be exposed to all dangers, to be devoured and harried by the teeth of wolves, whom they could not resist with this perversity of doctrine by which they had provoked them against themselves.




## 9.

But it is proved that sufficient answer has been made by your admonitions, so abounding in examples of our law. Nor have we thought that anything remains for us to say, since it is evident that nothing has been passed over by you, nothing suppressed, by which they may be known to be refuted and utterly convicted. And therefore no testimonies are set down by us, because in these things your report is full, and it is sufficiently evident that so many most learned priests have said everything: nor is it fitting to believe that you have passed over anything which could [0588C] profit the cause. *And in another hand:* Farewell, brethren. *And at the side:* Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [n: (Jan. 27 ann. 417)] after the consulship [nt: In the Corbie manuscript: *Luni Quarti*. In the Saint-Germain: *p. c. Theodosio augusto VII et Lucio Quarto v. consulibus*: from the ignorance of a copyist, who did not know that by the former note *p. c.* is signified *post consulatum*, and that therefore *Theodosii augusti*, etc., was to be kept, not *Theodosio augusto* substituted; and who did not know that the latter note, *v. c.*, was to be rendered by the words *viri clarissimi*, not by *v consulibus*.] of Theodosius Augustus for the seventh time and of Junius Quartus, V. C.

## EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 25. And what was 30 is now in the appendix.] XXX. OF POPE INNOCENT TO THE COUNCIL OF MILEVIS. *He praises the fathers of the council of Milevis, both because they judged that obstinate heretics were to be separated and the corrected to be received, and because, following the canons received everywhere, they sought the judgment of the apostolic see on anxious matters. Then he proves that the heresy which will have it that man can suffice to himself without the grace of God, and denies that baptism is necessary for little ones for eternal life, fights against the Scriptures. He orders its authors and their followers to be cut off from the Church, but to be received if they condemn their errors.*

*INNOCENT to SILVANUS the elder, VALENTINUS, [nt: It is the more probable that in this inscription Innocent addressed by name the individual bishops who had been named at the head of the letter of the council itself, because the only copies of this rescript that survive are those which, likewise in the preceding epistle, after naming Aurelius, indicated the other bishops under a general formula.] and the rest who were present at the synod of Milevis, most beloved brethren, greeting in the Lord.*

## I.

Among the other cares of the Roman church, and the occupations of the apostolic see, in which we treat the consultations of various persons with faithful and [nt: In the Roman edition and the Councils, from the Isidorian manuscripts: *modica*: a fault which Garnier, trying to correct it on his own, adds *non* before *modica*.] healing deliberation, our brother and fellow bishop Julius unexpectedly thrust upon me the letter of your charity [0589B] which you sent, with a more inclined care for the faith, from the council of Milevis, [nt: Only in copies of the Isidorian collection, and thence in Merlin and Crabbe: *ex Milevitano ex nostra auctoritate concilio*: a gloss worthy of Mercator, and deservedly removed in the Roman edition. As if indeed Innocent would have said that the letter of a council which had been assembled by his own authority had been thrust upon him unexpectedly.] adding also the writings of the synod of Carthage with a like complaint. Truly the Church exults that the shepherds show such solicitude for the flocks committed to them, that not only do they suffer none of them to go astray; but if the grass of a perverse [nt: Merlin: *sive*; Crabbe: *saevae*; the other editions of the Councils, after the Roman, and also Garnier: *obscaenae*; more rightly the other books: *scaerae*: which Labbe too noted in the margin. Next, the Isidorian manuscripts: *dilectionis*.] delight has rather led astray any of the sheep, they are willing either, if these remain in error, to have them wholly separated, or, if they avoid what they had long unlawfully sought, to protect them with the circumspection of their former keeping: taking counsel, that is, on both sides, lest either by receiving such, the others [nt: Quesnel: *seducantur*.] be led by a like example; or, by spurning those who return, these should seem to be thrown to the bites of wolves. Very prudent, and full of the catholic faith, is [nt: Garnier: *consolatio*. The Roman edition and the Councils, with the Isidorian manuscripts: *consultationis voluntas*. In one Colbert manuscript *consultationis* indeed stands, but *voluntas* is absent. More apt, as Quesnel has already observed, though a less Latin word, is *consultio*, which the other Colbert codex presents. By this name, then, is called that by which they take counsel for both sides, or use this counsel, neither to admit the obstinate nor to spurn those returning.] this counsel. For who could either tolerate [0589C] one who errs, or not receive [nt: In the Augustine edition: *se corrigentem*.] one who corrects himself? For as [0590A] I think it hard to show connivance to those who sin; so I judge it impious to refuse the hand to the converted.

## 2.

Diligently therefore and fittingly [nt: Garnier, with the Roman edition: *apostolico consulitis honori, honori*. Quesnel, following one Colbert manuscript: *apostolici consulitis honoris arcanis, honoris*. Nor does the other Colbert codex differ, except that for *arcanis* it has *arcani*. The Isidorian manuscripts: *apostolici consulitis honores arcani, honoris*. One of the Vatican manuscripts: *apostolici consulitis oneris arcana, oneris*. Sounder is the reading which we present here after the edition of the Councils and the Augustine edition. For this is what it means: you who consult the apostolic see, whose it is to disclose secret things. In the same manner of speaking Boniface I, epist. 5, n. 4, says *quae hujus consulis sedis arcanum*. Hence it is clear that *arcam* was wrongly written here in Crabbe's margin in place of the word *arcana*.] do you consult the secret counsels of the apostolic honour (of that honour, I say [sic: *in quam*], upon which, besides the things that are without, the care of all the churches waits) as to what judgment is to be held on anxious matters [n: (II Cor. XI, 28)]: following, that is, the form of the ancient rule, which you know, as I do, has always been kept by the whole world. But these things I let pass: for I do not believe that this is hidden from your prudence. [nt: So our manuscripts. The same sense is also given by what is in Merlin: *Qui id etiam actione firmastis, nisi scientes*. But the Roman edition and the Councils, after Crabbe: *quid id etiam*, with *nisi* then suppressed: which Quesnel likewise omits, preferring before it *quod etiam*. In the Augustine edition: *Qui id enim actione*, etc. In Garnier: *Cur id enim actione*, etc. If to anyone this, that *responses always flow from the apostolic fountain through all the provinces to those who ask*, should seem exaggerated, let him recall what Jerome wrote, epist. 110, now 91: *When I was helping Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, with ecclesiastical papers, and answering the synodical consultations of the East and of the West.*] Why have you also confirmed this by action, unless knowing that through all the provinces responses always flow from the apostolic fountain to those who ask? Especially [n: (24, q. 1, c. 12)] whenever the reason of the faith is discussed, I think that all our brethren and fellow bishops ought to refer to none but [0590B] Peter, that is, to the author of their name and honour, [nt: Inasmuch as from him the episcopate itself and the whole authority of this name arose, as he has it in the preceding epistle, n. 1; or, as Siricius says, epist. 5, n. 5, *through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate took their beginning in Christ*: which our Innocent too copies out, epist. 2, n. 2.] as your charity has now referred, what may profit all the churches in common throughout the whole world. For they must needs become more cautious, when they see the inventors of evils, on the report of a double synod, by the statutes of our judgment [nt: Quesnel alone: *se ab ecclesiastica communione sejungi*. Next Garnier: *fruetur*, for *fungetur*.] cut off from ecclesiastical communion. Your charity will therefore enjoy a twofold good. For you will both possess the grace of the canons observed, and the whole world will [nt: In the Roman edition and the Councils: *tutabitur*.] make use of your benefit. For who among catholic men would wish any longer to mingle speech with the adversaries of Christ? Who would share even the very light of life in common with them? [nt: The particle *cum* is put before it here in one manuscript.] Let the authors of the new heresy surely be shunned.

## 3.

For what more bitter could they feign against the Lord, [0590C] than when they made void the divine helps, and took away the cause [0591A] of daily prayer? This is to say, What need have I of God? Deservedly might the hymn-singer say against them: *Behold the men who did not make God their helper [var: Vulg. "Ecce homo qui non posuit," in the singular: Behold the man who did not make] [n: (Psalm. LI, 9)]*. Denying therefore the aid of God, they say that man can suffice to himself, and does not need divine grace: deprived of which, he must needs fall, entangled in the snares of the devil, while he strives for fulfilling all the commandments of life by his liberty alone. O perverse doctrine of most depraved minds! [nt: In the old editions of the Councils, as in the Augustine edition: *Advertat id tandem*. In the other printed editions and two manuscripts: *Adverte tandem*: which the epistle 21 of Celestine also favours, c. 7, where this passage is quoted thus: *Adverte tandem o pravissimarum mentium doctrina*. Wherefore, although the order of Innocent's words is changed there, yet on account of so ancient an authority we should incline to keep *adverte*, did not the train of the sentence resist it, in which one reads not *audi*, as Garnier and Quesnel edited against the manuscripts, but *audiat*. It pleases more, therefore, with some manuscripts, *advertens*, or *attendens*.] Noticing at last that liberty itself so deceived the first man that, while he used its reins too indulgently, he fell by presumption into transgression, [nt: Quesnel, with one Colbert manuscript: *praesumptionis*. Merlin and Crabbe, with the Isidorian manuscripts: *in praevaricationis praesumptione*.] and could not be rescued from it unless the coming of Christ the Lord had, by the providence of regeneration, restored [nt: Quesnel alone: *adventu*.] to him the state of his former liberty: let it hear David saying: [0591B] *Our help is in the name of the Lord [n: (Psalm. CXXIII, 8)]*; and, *Be thou my helper, forsake me not, neither despise me, O God my saviour [n: (Psalm. XXVI, 9)]*. Which he would have said in vain, if [nt: Garnier: *si totum*.] what he asked of the Lord with tearful speech had lain so fully in his own will.

## 4.

Since these things are so, and since in all the divine pages we read that nothing but the help of God is to be joined to the free will, and that it can do nothing when destitute of heavenly aids; in what manner do Pelagius and Coelestius, obstinately defending, as you assert, this possibility for it alone, persuade themselves, nay, what is [nt: In Quesnel: *gravius et dignius*. Then for *dolore communi* Garnier substitutes *dolore, communiter*. Then for the particle *jam*, which is suppressed in the Roman edition, *nam* wrongly stands in Merlin and Crabbe.] more worthy of common grief, already very many? We could indeed use manifold examples [nt: Two Colbert manuscripts: *ad instruendum*: which reading Merlin and Crabbe followed.] for destroying such a teaching, did we not know [0591C] that your holiness is fully versed in all the divine scriptures; especially since your report is so filled with so many and such testimonies, that by these alone the present doctrine could be cut down; and that there is no need of recondite ones, since they neither dare nor are able to oppose even those which you set down as readily occurring to you. So [nt: Garnier: *Ergone Dei*.] they try to take away the grace of God, which we must needs seek even when the liberty of our former state has been restored to us; since [nt: Quesnel: *quippe qui nec aliquas*; Garnier: *quippe nefarias*. Our manuscripts support neither.] we cannot avoid the other machinations of the devil either, except [0592A] with the same helping [n: (Augustin. lib. II, ad Bonifac., c. 4, n. 7)].

## 5.

But that which your fraternity asserts that they preach, that little ones can be rewarded with the prizes of eternal life even without the grace of baptism, is utterly foolish. For unless they eat the flesh of the son of man, and drink his blood, they shall not have life in themselves [n: (Joan. VI, 54)]. But those who defend this for them without regeneration seem to me to wish to make void baptism itself, since they preach that these have what is believed to be conferred on them only by baptism. If then they will have it that not to be reborn does no harm: they must needs confess that the sacred streams of regeneration are of no profit either. But, that the depraved doctrine of superfluous men may be ungirded by the swift reason [nt: So Quesnel and two Colbert manuscripts. But Merlin, with another Colbert manuscript: *distingui*: faultily. Nor better the other books: *discindi*. Silius too said *dolos ratione discingere*.] of truth, the Lord proclaims [0592B] this in the Gospel, saying: *Suffer the little ones, and forbid them [nt: Two Colbert manuscripts: *prohibere a me. Pro qua re Pelagium*.] not to come to me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven [var: Vulg. "pueros … regnum Dei," children … the kingdom of God] (Lucae XVIII, 16)*.

## 6.

## 4.

[0596A]But would that, what is rather to be wished, he may now turn himself from that error of his own track to the true way of the catholic faith, so that he may desire and wish to be cleared, considering the daily grace of God and acknowledging his help, so that he may be seen [nt: In Augustine, as in the manuscripts: *verum*. Shortly after, Labbe, following the Roman edition and Merlin: *gestorum judicio*: wrongly.] truly and be approved by all as corrected by manifest reason, not by the showing of acts, but with his heart turned to the catholic faith! If he is confident, and knows that what he says is not worthy of our condemnation, [nt: Quesnel, having put before this *Qui si se confidit*, here adds *ut confirmet verum esse quod dicat, aut etiam hoc totum*, etc., a mere gloss, which we have not found even in the old exemplars of the Codex he himself published. ## NOTICE ON THE THREE FOLLOWING LETTERS.



## 1.

The three following letters were first published at Rome among the pontifical letters from an old book of the Vatican library, and afterwards reprinted by Baronius too, at the year 416, after a collation of them had been made with another codex. Whence their first editor thought occasion was given for writing them he explains thus: « When John, bishop of Jerusalem, followed the errors of Origen, Jerome, living at Bethlehem, and very many others abstained from his communion. For which reason, through the work of John, they were afflicted with many evils. » But we have learned the truer cause of them from what Augustine relates at the close of the book On the Proceedings of Pelagius, in this manner: « But concerning those things which after this judgment (held at Diospolis in Palestine) are said to have been perpetrated there with incredible audacity by I know not what band of abandoned men, who are said to favour Pelagius in a very [0598B] perverse way, so that the servants and handmaids of God belonging to the care of holy Jerome were afflicted with most wicked slaughter, a deacon was killed, the buildings of the monasteries were burned, and he himself was scarcely protected from this onset and incursion of the impious, in the mercy of God, by a more fortified tower, I see that we must rather be silent, and wait to see what our brethren the bishops there think should be done about these great evils, which who would believe they could pass over? » For it is clear that the evils described in the letters subjoined were suffered by Jerome not at all from the Origenists but from the Pelagians.



## 2.

From the same account we learn that the irruption of these heretics into the monastery committed to Jerome's care happened after the synod of Diospolis. Whence it follows that it by no means took place at the time when Jerome was abstaining from John's communion. For in the year 415, as the month of December was running out, the synod of Palestine, or of Diospolis, [0598C] was held. But from the year 397 the learned prove that John had been reconciled with Jerome through the work of Theophilus of Alexandria. [n: (V. Tillem. tom. XII, p. 199.)] From the same place it is also manifest that the following letters were by no means written before the year 416. But neither does the death of John, recorded at the year 417, allow them to be much later than this year. By Baronius they are referred to the end [0599A] of the year 416. But he ought to have gathered from Epistle 33 itself that they are to be put off to the year 417. For Aurelius, to whom this letter is inscribed, and through whom Jerome wished his letters to be delivered to Innocent, and in turn Innocent wished those in which he wrote back to Jerome to be delivered to him, he judges to be none other than the bishop of [sic: *Cathaginensi*] Carthage; nor does anyone oppose him in this matter. But in truth, when this Aurelius with his colleagues wrote at the beginning of the year 417 to Innocent against Pelagius and Coelestius, he did not know that Jerome had suffered anything from the satellites of these heretics. At that time it was only noised abroad in Africa that Pelagius, established at Jerusalem, was deceiving many there, but that many more, of whom in the letter of the synod of Milevis Jerome alone is named, « were contending against him for the grace of Christ and the truth of the catholic faith. » Certainly this place called for the addition also of what the new defender of the grace of Christ had borne from the impious, if knowledge of so atrocious a crime had reached Africa. It is not to be doubted, however, that [0599B] that most keen conflict of Jerome against Pelagius was the true cause why he was dealt with so cruelly. Although, therefore, Eustochium and Paula had kept silent about the cause and the author of the violence brought upon their monastery, yet it was not difficult for Innocent, forewarned of what Pelagius was busy doing at Jerusalem, to scent this out.

## 3.

This pope rebuked John of Jerusalem with letters so threatening, not only because it was his part either to restrain or to punish such great crimes, but also because perhaps a suspicion was not lacking that he had favoured them. The old enmities between him and Jerome on the cause of Origen, although long since laid to rest, were not hidden. He had also heard, as report announced, how greatly Pelagius was loved by John. Wherefore Augustine, epist. 179, no. 1, addresses John himself thus: « But Pelagius our brother, thy son, whom I hear that thou lovest much; » and in no. 5: « If you love Pelagius, let him also love you, nay rather himself, [0599C] and not deceive you. »

## 4.

Lastly we observe that the letter of Innocent to this John savours of Greek phrasing: and therefore that this pope either wrote in Greek, or at least took care that what he had written in Greek should be turned into Latin, and that only the Latin interpretation of this Greek text, very tenacious of the letter, has come down to us. Certainly one or another place which at first sight appears obscure or even maimed, when brought to the Greek phrasing, at once comes out clear and whole.

## EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 34; the one which was 33 is now 34.] XXXIII. *Innocent sends Aurelius a letter to be delivered to Jerome.*

[0600A]

*INNOCENT TO HIS MOST BELOVED BROTHER AURELIUS.*

Our fellow presbyter Jerome did well to believe in thy most pious affection for coming [nt: Some persuade themselves from this, following Baronius, that the letters of Jerome, as also of Eustochium and Paula, to Innocent were carried by Aurelius himself. Yet this Aurelius is mentioned here as having the affection for coming into the City, not as having come. Nor, if he had been present in person, would there have been need of these letters. We should therefore think it better that he took pains to have them carried by one of his own people.] to us. We suffer with a member of our flock, and what we thought should be done, or were able to do, we have speedily carried out. Let thy brotherhood, dearest brother, make haste to deliver the letter all the sooner to the aforementioned ( *Jerome* ).

## EPISTLE [nt: In the edition of the Councils, 32; the one which was 34 is now 33.] XXXIV. *Innocent consoles Jerome for what he has suffered, and declares what he has thought should be done for the present, and has already done.*

*INNOCENT TO HIS MOST BELOVED SON JEROME, PRESBYTER.* [0600B]

The Apostle testifies that contention has never done any good in the Church; and therefore he bids that the rebukes of heretics be made first rather [nt: So we had thought it should be corrected, because it had been published thus with no sense, nay with a sense contrary to Innocent's mind, as *magisque diuturna*, when our conjecture was confirmed by a re-examination of the Vatican archetype itself, and we learned that the fault had arisen from the mere unskilfulness of a copyist in reading old books. While this rule is carelessly regarded, [nt: Baronius, having thrown *aspicitur* out to the margin of the book (which here is the same as *consideratur*), substituted *accipitur* in the text.] the evil which is to be guarded against is not avoided, but increased. It will be more complete if one reads *ut nulla ratio*.] there is reason for not treating and consulting: first I address the faith of thy constancy. That everyone, for the truth, is struck with injury or, as thou sayest, with danger, [nt: In the edition of the Councils, after Baronius: *qui exspectat*. *Augustine continues [n: (Ibid., c. 31)]*: *When he had mixed in with these invidious complaints about his enemies, he comes to the matter thus:* Behold, let this letter clear me before thy beatitude, in which purely and simply we say that we have whole free will for sinning and for not sinning, which in all good works is always helped by divine aid.

## 3.

*Then, says Augustine [n: (Ibid.,)]*, *having interposed certain things about the condition of man, and about his natural possibility of sinning and of not sinning, he added:* [0609A] Which power of free will we say is in all generally, in Christians, in Jews and in Gentiles. In all free will is equally by nature: but in Christians alone it is helped by grace. In the former the good of their condition is naked and unarmed: but in these who belong to Christ it is fortified by the help of Christ. The former are to be judged and condemned because, since they have free will, through which they could come to faith and merit [nt: On these words Augustine: "Plainly, he says, it is manifest that he says grace is given according to merits, whatever or whatsoever kind of grace he means; which however he does not openly express."] the grace of God, they make ill use of the liberty granted. But these are to be rewarded who, making good use of free will, merit the grace of the Lord and keep his commandments.



## 4.

Likewise he challenged his adversaries to the reading of the books which he had written earlier, in these words [0609B] [n: (Ibid., c. 35)]: « Let them read that letter [nt: To these Augustine again subjoins: "This I have read; and I found that through almost the whole of it he dwells on nothing but the faculty and possibility of nature, and places the grace of God almost there alone. But Christian grace he touches with such brevity that he seems to have done nothing else than to have feared to be silent about it."], which we wrote to the holy man Paulinus, bishop, almost twelve years ago, which in perhaps three hundred lines confesses nothing else than the grace and help of God, and that we can do nothing at all of good without God. Let them read also the letter [nt: Augustine testifies that he could not find this. "But if, he says, it is not unlike the others, it too has not what we are looking for."] to the holy bishop Constantius [n: (Ibid., c. 36)], where briefly indeed, but plainly, I joined the grace and help of God to the free will of man. Let them read also the one which [nt: Of this the same Doctor speaks thus: "This indeed I have read, and it had almost persuaded me that he confesses that grace which is in question. But when other things too had come into my hands, which he wrote later and more at large, I saw how he could have named grace even there, hiding what he thought under an ambiguous generality, yet breaking the odium and declining offence by the word grace." And Augustine laid bare the poison lurking in this work of Pelagius in the epistle formerly 143, now 188, to Juliana, at the end of which letter he marks, not obscurely, this letter of Pelagius to Innocent, nay this very passage, where he says: "But in a certain letter of his, where the same Pelagius both puts his own name most openly and does not keep silent the name of the sacred virgin, he says that he wrote to her, and tries to prove by the testimony of that same work of his that he most openly confesses the grace of God, which he is asserted either to keep silent or to deny."] we wrote in the East to Demetrias, the sacred virgin of Christ [n: (Ibid., c. 37)]: and they will find that we so praise the nature of man that we always add the help of the grace of God. Let them read also my recent [nt: Of this little work this is Augustine's judgment: "There are four books of this work, and I have read them... But in these four books also, whatever he seems to say in favour of the grace by which we are helped to turn aside from evil and to do good, he so says that he in no way departs from verbal ambiguity, which he can so explain to his disciples that they believe in no help of grace by which the possibility of nature is aided, except in the law and teaching." And after a few things left out: "But this help of law and teaching he judges to have existed in the times of the prophets too, while the help of grace, which is properly called grace, he judges to consist in the example of Christ; which you perceive nonetheless belongs to teaching, which is preached to us as the gospel."] little work [n: (Ibid., c. 41)], which we were lately compelled to publish on behalf of free will: and they will recognize how unjustly they have been eager to defame us with the denial [0609C] of grace, we who through almost the whole text of that very work perfectly and entirely confess both free will and grace. » [0610A]

## 5.

But from this letter too he wishes the reader to pass over to the book of his faith, which he had subjoined to it [n: (Ibid., c. 32)]. This book of faith, moreover, is inserted whole in the Sermon formerly of Augustine *de Tempore* 191, now appendix 236, n. 2 and following, and besides has been published separately in the appendix of vol. X of the new edition of the same saint, page 96, as also among the works of Jerome, to whom it had once been ascribed.

## 6.

Moreover in that letter, « which, » says Augustine [n: (lib. de Peccato origin., n. 19, 20 et 21)] , « he sent to Rome to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, and since they did not find him in the body, it was given to holy Pope Zosimus, and directed to me, that is, in the same letter, he complained » that he was defamed [nt: To this Augustine, in the place cited: "These things are not objected to them as he has put it. For they neither deny to little ones the sacrament of baptism, nor promise the kingdom of heaven to some without the redemption of Christ... But it is objected to them that they will not confess that unbaptized little ones are liable to the condemnation of the first man."] by men, as though he denied to little ones the sacrament of baptism, and promised to some the kingdom [0610B] of heaven without the redemption of Christ. » And when he had said « that he had never heard even any impious heretic who would say this of little ones, » he went on: « For who is so ignorant of the reading of the Gospel as not only to attempt to affirm this, but who could even lightly say it or even think it? Next, who so impious as to wish little ones to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, while he forbids [nt: About to bring forward these words of Pelagius, Augustine puts before them: "See him preparing hiding-places of ambiguity as refuges for falsehood, pouring darkness over the truth; so that even we, when we first read these things, almost rejoiced at them as right or corrected. But his broader disputations in his books, he says, where, however much he may cover himself, he is mostly compelled to uncover himself, made even these things suspect to us, so that, looking into them more attentively, we found them ambiguous."] them to be baptized and reborn in Christ, and forbids [nt: Having explained how much Augustine laboured over the understanding of these words, he adds: "They are so ambiguous that they could afford hiding-places for their doctrine, from which the heretical sense might leap out to lie in wait."] him who was born to an uncertain life to be reborn to a perpetual and certain one. »

## 7.

Together with the aforesaid letter of Pelagius and his little book of faith there was sent to Innocent, and together delivered to Innocent's successor Zosimus, the letter of Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, of which we learn this one thing from Zosimus, that in it Praylius, John's successor, intervened as a very earnest supporter of the cause [0610C] of Pelagius [n: (Epist. 3, n. 2)].

## 8.

But whoever reads the aforesaid [0611A] fragments of the letter of Pelagius, and weighs also the observations subjoined by Augustine, who knew well all the arts and subterfuges of this crafty heretic, and hears at the same time that the same man was approved and praised by the commendation of the prelate of Jerusalem, will surely wonder the less that Zosimus, receiving his words simply as they sounded, could be deceived by him.

## NOTICE ON THE FRAGMENT FOLLOWING.[n: (Spicileg. Maii, tom. III.)]

To the letters of Innocent I above, published often, we subjoin a larger part of his unpublished letter to Severian, bishop of Gabala. Indeed in the Arabic codex *Haiala* is written, not *Gabala*, a reading which receives some force from the fact that *Aila* is an episcopal city of Palestine in Le Quien, Or. ch. vol. III, p. 758; but yet among the very few bishops of that city whom [0611B] Le Quien knew, Severian is not counted. I therefore thought at once of Severian, bishop of Gabala, likewise a Syrian city, who was a contemporary of Innocent; and, what matters more, we learn in the notice of the lost letters of Innocent in Coustant, p. 921, that letters passed back and forth between Severian and Innocent. Besides, a little below in the Arabic codex a fragment likewise of Severian is read, in which place his episcopal see is called not *Haiala* but *Gabala*. The fault of the Arabic codex therefore arose from the likeness of a small letter. Let us then gratefully accept this fragment of a letter of Innocent, preserved for us by an Arab.

## EPISTLE XLIII. OR FRAGMENT OF THE LETTER WHICH INNOCENT, ONE OF THE FIRST BISHOPS OF ROME, WROTE TO BISHOP SEVERIAN.

[0611C]When the divine Word came from heaven, and dwelt in the womb of the holy Virgin Mary, from whom he took flesh, he by no means brought his body [0612A] with him from heaven, nor did he acquire his divinity on earth; but he himself was God, he himself formed his body in the Virgin's womb; nor did he have any partner in making his body, but he alone made it. And we confess that in all things which were done by the humanity the divinity was its companion, which was never separated from the humanity by any moment of time, not even the least. We confess also that at the very time when our Saviour came from heaven and descended into the womb of the Virgin Mary, he joined the divinity with the humanity, which were never divided in any thing or action, since they were indivisible. And just as his divinity lacks end, so also his humanity remains for ever after the resurrection. He sucked milk from a woman; nonetheless the divinity [0612B] and the humanity constituted one ( *Christ* ). Nor let anyone think that at the time when the divine Word on earth came to receive baptism from John, the beginning of his divinity was then, when, namely, John heard the voice of the Father coming out of heaven. It is by no means so; but at the very moment of time at which he descended into the Virgin's womb, one indivisible thing was made with the body and the divinity; and the divinity was the consort of the body, and in a certain immutable and inseparable manner a single unity was made. The divinity is not separated from the humanity. When Christ was on the cross, the divinity did not withdraw from his humanity. He ascended into heaven with the body which he took from the Virgin Mary, and sat at the right hand of his most good Father. This is our [0612C] faith. But those who do not so believe, the catholic Church expels them, nay its author, God, excommunicates them. Praise be to God for ever! Amen.
